He wanted to live. He still desperately wanted to live... everyone else could die, but he had to survive. There were so many things he regretted. So many things he could still do...

He tried to move away from the creature, but it was already too late.

Something flashed in the air, and suddenly, he felt lighter.

His vision grew blurry.

The snow was painted red.

Red... like the proud banners of the Empire. Like the glorious color of war.

Glory! Glory! Glory!

'Move, I must... move...'

There was no pain.

He fell down, and the dark expanse of the night sky swallowed his vision.

Growing darker and darker with each moment.

Like a vast, impossible shadow.

That was the last thing he saw.

...Deep in the cave, the shadow let out a sigh.

'Why do people love life so much?'

What was so lovable about its vicious, cruel splendor?

Perhaps it was simply in their nature. They were the Creatures of the Flame, after all... the Flame of Desire.

And the desire to be alive was the most ancient and powerful of all.

--- Chapter 3167 ---

The boundless black sky was the last thing that the lost soldier had seen in his bitter, senseless life.

However, that was not the end of it.

The man had lived for a minute or two more... what had been the man, at least... and the shadow had lived those minutes with him. However, it did not want to remember those last moments — they were a vessel of Corruption, after all, and the shadow had no desire to feel the seeds of darkness bloom in its soul again.

Uprooting them was quite a hassle.

It remained motionless, hidden in the depths of the cave, the vivid memories of a past life still echoing in its mind. Everything about that life was so vibrant, so sharp, so stark... so different from its current peaceful existence. The shadow did not want to suffer the sharpness of life anymore.

And yet, it could not help but remember.

The lost soldier had disdained Shadow God, thinking that a deity who would allow its temples to burn was not worthy of reverence. There was no trace of the Shadow cult left in the vast and glorious Empire, after all.

However, he failed to realize that the Empire of War, while great and splendid, existed only in the world of the living... and life was nothing but a fleeting dream in the face of death.

Death was eternal, after all.

A life that spanned a scattering of years or the eternity of death... which one seemed insignificant? And why would Shadow God care about the fact that those who served War had forgotten their reverence for him, if their lives in the Empire were merely a brief stop on the way to the Realm of Shadows?

The shadow sighed.

It understood death better than the lost soldier had. And yet, it still couldn't forget the fleeting brilliance of life.

And so, uninvited, the memories of another life — one very similar to the first one, but also entirely different — surfaced from the deep ocean of its vague, fragmented memories.

In that life, he had been unfortunate. He was unfortunate because he was born at the periphery of the Empire, in one of the distant lands the legions of War had conquered.

The people who lived there were subjects of the Empire, but they were not its citizens. The glamour and splendor of the imperial heartland was like a myth to them, and they spent their lives toiling not to starve.

He came from a family of serfs. They did not own the land they farmed, and most of what they harvested was taken away by the governor of a nearby fortress. They weren't slaves, of course — they were free men and women. The distance between them and those wearing a collar was as vast as the sea.

At least that was what they told themselves, looking at the slaves tending the land of rich folks with disdain.

He did not know how vast the sea was, anyway. He had never seen the sea... in fact, he had never seen anything beyond his family's small plot of land and the nearby village.

Still, it wasn't a bad life. It might have been harsh and full of hard labor, but they rarely went hungry. He and his siblings might have all shared a small room, but at least they slept on soft mats, not on rough straw.

All of them, except for the youngest ones, woke up at dawn to help their father in the field. Their mother would already have their breakfast ready, and after eating their fill and thanking her, they left through the flimsy door of their modest home.

The door was painted red, and there was a silver bell hanging above the porch. When the wind blew, it rang beautifully.

In the moments of sweet leisure, that ringing accompanied him.

But, still...

He wanted more.

He had not even known that he wanted more, or what it meant to want anything, until he saw the soldiers march one day. Their plot was situated near the imperial road, and once in a while, the legionnaires would march past it, a river of red banners billowing above them.

He was small and weak. Toiling in the soil, he was covered in mud. His clothes were rough and colorless, threadbare, while his body was gaunt and frail. The soldiers, however...

The imperial soldiers were everything he was not.

They were tall and mighty. Their garments were painted with vibrant dye, and their armor glistened brilliantly in the sun. To a serf child like him, they were the epitome of wonder, of brilliance... of pride.

Of the Empire.

He became obsessed with everything having to do with the Empire after seeing the soldiers for the first time. Opportunities to learn were few and far between in the remote corner of the province, but there were still stories and legends. There were still wandering priests telling myths about the Spirits of the Empire.

It was from that that he learned about the valiant Spirit of Victory, the guardian deity of soldiers, who was a descendant of the Dragon and a warrior of unmatched skill.

He learned about the Spirit of Beauty, the Sacred Maiden, as well — the deity of perseverance, harvests, and motherhood.

The Spirit of Art, whose brilliance and ingenuity ensured the prosperity of the Empire, was the patron of all craftsmen and artisans.

And finally, there was the Spirit of Joy — the carefree deity of festivity and merrymaking.

He learned about the Supremes who ruled the Empire, too — the High Priests and Priestesses of the Cult of War. Each of them was a famed hero whose deeds had long become legends.

How wondrous they were, how marvelous... how dreamlike.

And, of course, there was the Dragon.

The Dragon, who dwelled atop a great tower in the heart of the Empire — a tower so tall that it scratched the sky and imposed on the realm of Sun God.

The Dragon, a living vessel of War God, had founded the Empire and oversaw it in its early years. He still watched over his subjects from his empyrean throne, his fearsome gaze scaring other deities and the Creatures of Corruption away.

Of course, War God did not rule the Empire personally anymore. The days of gods walking the earth were long over, left in the mythical Ages of Gods and Heroes.

This was a golden age — the Age of Humans.

But, of course...

Watching the glorious soldiers march past the small farm, he couldn't help but imagine that, one day... just perhaps... he could become a hero, too.

Time passed, and he grew from a boy into a young man. His family's small home seemed even smaller now, and the plot of land they toiled on seemed even more pathetic.

So, in the end, going against the wishes of his parents, he left in hopes of joining the imperial legion.

The wind was strong on the day he abandoned home. As he walked away, leaving his parents and siblings behind, the ringing of the silver bell pursued him like a sonorous song... following an impulse, he took it off the strings and placed it with his things.

He was lucky. Usually, it wasn't easy for someone like him — an untrained youth from a remote outer province — to join the great and glorious imperial army. But the Empire was gearing up for a new campaign, and so, the legions needed fresh bodies.

The competition for a spot in one of the legions was still fierce — how could it not be, when becoming a soldier promised not only riches and glory, but also a direct path to becoming a citizen? — but he performed well in front of the recruiters. His frame was tall, as well, and he was no stranger to hard work.

And so, his new life as a soldier began.

At first, he often missed home. The bell he carried in his pack reminded him of the warm days of his childhood... of his mother's touch, of his siblings laughing. Of a brighter, more innocent time. At night, he would hold it tightly and remember the past.

But as time went on, he reached for the bell less and less. Its ringing didn't sound sweet to him anymore... instead, he grew to enjoy the ringing of sharp steel.

Surviving his first war was a challenge. The second... he was seasoned by then, having become a tempered blade of the Empire. The third one was when he had proven himself and was elevated to the rank of centurion.

The army gave him what he had always felt he lacked — the right to hold his head high. To be proud of himself. To know that he was an important part of something great and fearsome.

Of something glorious.

He had left his family behind, but the Empire replaced it. The Spirits were his parents, and the fellow soldiers were his siblings. Out there on the battlefield, he never felt alone.

Sadly, there wasn't always war.

The Empire had existed for a thousand years already, and there were few places where its legions hadn't reached.

The barbarous, inferior wretches that populated them lacked the courage to offer proper resistance.

Building pathways to previously unconquered realms took time and resources.

At best, the soldiers would be sent to suppress an occasional uprising in one of the newer provinces. At worst, they were left to rot and die of boredom in the fortresses, with no opportunity to elevate themselves in battle or engage in the many pleasures of war.

His dreams of becoming a hero had been crushed, as well. Despite all the years that had passed, he wasn't even close to becoming an Awakened. And so, his career prospects grew dim.

Even though he tried to crush the dark thoughts, at times, he couldn't help but feel bitter. He couldn't help but resent who was better than him, younger than him... stronger than him.

And yet, his devotion to the Spirit of Victory and to the Dragon, as well as to the Empire itself, never wavered. In fact, it only became more fanatical.

He wasn't young by then, and had accumulated plenty of merit. If he wanted to, he could retire and live a comfortable life in the heartland of the Empire as its citizen — in fact, many of his comrades already had.

...Soon, it was most of them.

But the thought of retiring from the soldier's life had never even crossed his mind. Even when his hair turned grey, and his body began to falter, he remained stalwart in his devotion to serving the Empire.

Because the Empire was his god.

It was also because he didn't know anything except the harsh embrace of the imperial legions. The world outside his service was strange and unfamiliar. Everything had changed, at some points... the roads he marched on, the cities he encountered, the people he met. All of it was new, and it felt like the world was passing him by. Had already left him behind, lost in the dust. Only the Spirits and the Dragon remained the same, like the axis of the world.

He loved them for it.

Retiring? Living comfortably in some peaceful town? Starting a family of his own and nursing children?

He had no desire for such life. He had no interest in the softness of soil. All he desired was the harshness of steel.

Eventually, his age caught up with him, and the kind of orders he received changed. That was how he ended up leading a caravan that escorted shackled convicts — the lowest of the low, each and every one of them.

Despicable slaves...

The mission wasn't too difficult for a seasoned veteran like him. Apart from keeping the slaves in check and teaching the new recruits not to get cozy with them, there wasn't much to do. Still, he maintained his vigilance.

He always did.

He had participated in the suppression of a slave rebellion once or twice, after all. These lowlifes outnumbered him and his soldiers ten to one — he knew all too well what happened when wicked thoughts entered their bestial heads, and he knew how easily those iron shackles came off.

The real chain that bound them — the only one that could — was not made from iron. It was made from fear. It was made from surrender and submission, so he made sure to keep the slaves from thinking about anything else but his whip.

Still, even his vigilance had a limit.

The danger came from an unexpected source. It was not the disobedient slaves, road bandits, or even the elements — it came from higher up the mountain, taking the shape of a ghastly Creature of Corruption.

He knew that this would be where he died the moment he saw the beast.

The imperial legions were no strangers to fighting the Corrupted, of course, and he had participated in his fair share of battles against these insidious foes. So, he immediately knew that the beast was of a high Class... he and his mundane soldiers could have handled a Beast or two, perhaps even a Monster. But this creature?

It was death.

Still, he wasn't going to give up without a fight.

If he was to die, he was going to die while holding a sword, like he had all his life.

He was going to die hearing the clangor of steel.

The battle was short.

At the end of it all, he found himself lying in the snow. He didn't remember how he had gotten there, or what had happened to his soldiers.

There was no strength in his body. He couldn't move.

He was so cold.

He was cold and alone, surrounded by silence. All he could see was the night sky, and the snowflakes drifting slowly from the boundless darkness above.

He was dying.

It took all his remaining strength to turn his head. Out there, in the snow, he noticed the hilt of his sword. The blade was broken, but it was still a sword... his sword...

It was a sword of the Empire, just like he was.

He tried to reach for it, but his hand didn't move.

‘Must... must...’

He had to take it. He had to... he wanted to... die while holding that familiar hilt.

But it was of no use.

He grew desperate. He grew weak.

His thoughts turned slow and cold, just like the bloodied world.

He reached for the sword harder than for anything ever before...

But, still, his hand refused to move.

Angry tears moistened his eyes, growing cold in the frigid air.

Then, a shadow fell on him.

Moving his eyes, he saw a gaunt boy standing above him, his pale face expressionless. In the pale moonlight, his skin looked like pure alabaster, and his dark eyes were like two pieces of obsidian.

For a moment, he was frightened that it was Death. He was scared that Shadow God had come to take him to the lightless realm, broken and unarmed... no different from the wretched slaves that had died on the slope of the mountain while trying to run away from the beast.

No, no...

The boy was merely one of the slaves.

The wretch was still alive, having come to gloat.

He gritted his teeth, wanting to feel fury. Wanting to curse the pathetic worm.

But he was too tired. He was too cold to feel anything.

Even his despair was gone. All that was left was a sense of weakness and resignation. His life was like a candle's flame, ready to go out.

He stared at the boy, and the boy studied him silently.

Then, the boy knelt beside him and picked up the broken sword.

Reaching down, the boy raised one of his unfeeling hands, placed the hilt into it, and put it on his chest.

He found some strength to grip the hilt tightly, looking at the boy with surprise. And gratitude.

Expressionless, the boy let go of his hand and stood. Then, turning away, he disappeared into darkness.

There was silence then.

He lay in the snow, gripping his sword tightly, breathing his last breaths.

Death was coming.

‘Sword... my... sword...’

His sword was finally in his hand, but at that moment, for some reason, he didn't feel like he had missed its touch.

Instead, he remembered a different weight. The modest weight of a silver bell he had held often, a long time ago.

‘Right... the bell...‘

When had he lost it?

He didn't remember.

He had not thought about that thing for years, but now that it was gone, he suddenly felt its absence.

He could almost hear its ringing.

Its sweet ringing...

As it swayed in the wind on a sunlit porch. Now, there was only silence left.

Only darkness.

The sword fell from his motionless hand.

...The shadow surfaced from the torrent of memories, feeling like it had been drowning.

At some point, without thinking about it, it had taken a shape.

That shape was rough and vague, but still resembled a human.

The clear ringing of the silver bell echoed in his mind.

He felt like he could almost touch it...

Looking down, at his black hand, the shadow was surprised to see a small silver bell lying in his palm, having appeared there as if by magic.

‘Where did...’

He frowned in confusion, then raised the small silver bell and studied it closely. Then, following a strange impulse, the shadow rang it.

--- Chapter 3168 ---

The clear ringing of the bell resounded in the dark cave, straining to escape it. The shadow willed it to stay within the stone walls of his shelter, sensing the sound reverberating through him.

As a peculiar vibration was born in his chest, he remembered.

The courtyard of a dark, magnificent temple that stood under a lightless sky. The rustle of leaves washing over him as a towering tree swayed gently in the wind. The laughter of a young woman who sat on the ground, enjoying a lavish picnic...

The memory came and went, leaving behind a lasting ache. The shadow did not like the feeling, so he put the silver bell down and collapsed back into his natural, formless state.

Fleeing from it.

His thoughts were heavy.

What had come over him, anyway? Taking the form of a human... who would want to be a ghastly being like that?

It was the memories of the two men who died on the slopes of the lonesome mountain, no doubt. The two of them had lived similar lives, but went down entirely different paths. By the end, the gap separating them was as wide as the abyss. And yet, they died on the same day, with only a few meters between them, their blood mixing in the snow.

The shadow remembered being those men. He remembered being the abomination who had slain them, as well.

He even remembered being the worm who had created the abomination, using the mind of a distrustful king as its chrysalis. All those lives, all those deaths... they were there, hidden in the depths of the shadow's mind.

But he did not want to recall them.

So, instead, the shadow cast his senses far and wide, so that the empty state of being fused with the world erased his thoughts. So that he could forget.

Oblivion was the only solace to those who were denied death, it seemed.

Time passed, but no matter how much the shadow tried to return to his previous peaceful non-existence, fragments of memories kept creeping into his mind.

He remembered...

Living as a soldier in a lightless land. The world was besieged by darkness, and in its cold embrace, those who still lived had to fight desperately to survive. He fought for the right to exist, as well...

He was a warrior of the Starlight Legion.

His people were led by seven great heroes who had risen to the heights of power in the endless war against the darkness... as well as the awful beings that dwelled under its tenebrous veil. Under their guidance, the humans slowly pushed the detestable creatures back, coming together to build an impregnable city in the heart of the forsaken land.

The gods were dead, so they had no one to pray to. The sun was gone, so there was nothing to illuminate their path. Even the stars had vanished from the sky, having fallen down like flaming tears.

He did not know what the sun looked like, since he had been born after the darkness devoured the world. He did not know what the stars looked like, either. But he had heard the stories... he had dreamed countless times about their distant radiance, about the sea of silver light shining brightly in the boundless black sky.

He wanted to see the stars before he died. That was the goal of the Starlight Legion.

Death was a constant companion to the soldiers of the legion. Many of them perished on the battlefield, and few survived long enough to leave a lasting mark.

He was one of the few.

He had survived many battles, slain many abominations, and buried many comrades. The longer he lived, the stronger he became. Eventually, other soldiers came to rely on him as their brother...

But death wasn't the worst fate for those who fought under the banner of the Starlight Legion. They spent their lives surrounded by darkness, after all, and the darkness seeped into them slowly, year after year, pooling in their souls.

It began from an itch. A maddening itch that came and went, but could never be entirely chased away. Peculiar thoughts soon started to enter his mind. Sometimes, he caught himself looking at his fellow soldiers or at the civilians back home, thinking how soft their bodies were. How red their blood was.

He was thirsty.

At times, no amount of water could quench his thirst. He felt like he was burning in the middle of the desert, dying in unbearable heat.

He longed to dive into the embrace of a cold, dark sea.

One day, the itch drove him mad enough to shred his forearm in a frenzy. As drops of red, vibrant, fragrant blood fell to the floor, he froze and stared at the gruesome wound in shock and revulsion.

There was something there, hidden in the bleeding flesh.

Reaching into the wound with calloused fingers, he pulled a thin, translucent plate from within his forearm.

It was scale.

There were scales and filaments growing under his skin, propagating slowly. Shuddering, he dropped the scale, took a step back, and tried to suppress the desire to sever his entire arm.

In the end, he bandaged the wound, glanced around his tent, and thought of his modest home back in the city.

He was never going to come home again, it seemed.

Following the oaths, he reported himself to the capellan of the cohort. The rest happened quickly.

He was not the first among the warriors of the Starlight Legion to succumb to the curse of the darkness, after all — far from it. Those like him, the veterans who had been infected by the darkness, were all assigned to a special unit. They lived like lepers, isolated from the rest of the soldiers and hiding their gruesome bodies under layered bandages.

However, they were not quite useless yet. On the contrary, he and the others marked by the darkness were always the ones to take on the most perilous missions, to fight where the battle was most harrowing, to die so that the others could live.

Even if the darkness had seeped into their souls and bodies, they were its most fearsome foes. If one of them died on the battlefield, they celebrated. If one was too stubborn to be killed by the claws and fangs of detestable creatures, and the curse progressed too far... then they would bring their comrade mercy with steel blades.

That blade of his, forged from azure steel, had slain numerous monsters.

It had slain plenty of his brothers, as well... Time passed, but he still failed to die. His body was a ghastly wreck by then, and his face was not worthy of showing to a mirror. He felt like the day when his siblings of the Starlight Legion would have to deliver him a final mercy was approaching soon.

That was when their hero, the Warrior, had come to meet them.

He entrusted them with one final mission... a sacred mission. A harrowing mission that only they were fit to carry out.

On a day like any other — all days were the same in the world without a sun, after all — they came to surround a vast crowd of people. There were warriors of the legion there, but there were peaceful citizens, as well. Men and women, old and young — those whom they had sworn to protect. They surrounded the crowd.

And when the ritual began — one of the seven being carried out across the lightless land — they drew their blades and turned them on the people.

They slaughtered them all in a great hecatomb. They killed until the world itself was painted red, until their arms fell limp from exhaustion, until there was no one left alive.

Until no trace of azure remained on the surface of his loyal sword.

The Warrior was there, as well. He was the last to die, sacrificing himself on the altar of his ardent mission.

Of an oath to return light into the lightless sky.

...When everything was over, he swayed and leaned heavily on his sword, looking in a daze at the corpses littering the bloodsoaked ground. He was tired. He was overcome with sorrow.

He mourned the death of his people.

He mourned himself, as well.

And, most of all, he mourned the death of his hero.

Overcome by grief, he looked up...

And saw the sun being born in the black sky.

Ever since he was a child, he had heard countless descriptions of the sun. He knew that it was round. He knew that it was so bright as to appear white — like the purest of flames. He knew that it illuminated the world, making colors vivid and all things clear.

But no description could have prepared him for how brilliant the sun was.

For how beautiful the world was in its blinding light.

Its radiance chased away the darkness, and suddenly, the black abyss above was not black anymore. It was a clear, vibrant blue. And below it, on the ground, the blood was suddenly unbearably red.

As he looked at the radiant sun, blinded by its incandescent brilliance, tears flowed down his face.

"A star... it is a star..."

A star was burning in the sky.

He finally saw it.

However, he did not feel joy.

He only felt shame and sorrow.

In the blinding radiance of the newborn sun, the darkness that dwelled in his soul only grew more impenetrable. All around him, his fellow soldiers suddenly convulsed and screamed.

He screamed, as well.

He fell to his knees, shrieking, his body bending and breaking.

Thick plates of chitin covered his skin, encasing him within an impenetrable carapace. Scythe-like limbs tore his flesh apart, piercing the ground like fearsome blades. His figure twisted, expanding, transforming...

Until there was nothing of him left.

The last thing he saw before the darkness swallowed him was his sword, lying in the filth on the ground, its azure blade desecrated and painted dark crimson by blood.

He knew that one day, soon, all memories of him would be erased from the world. All traces of him, and the Starlight Legion as well, would be gone, and everything they had done — both their valor and their sin — would be forgotten.

Only steel would remain.

Only steel would remember.

At the end there, he felt regret.

He thought that his poor, loyal sword deserved to forget as well...

--- Chapter 3169 ---

The shadow surfaced from the memory. But he also drowned in it.

The slave, the slave driver, the warrior of a lightless land... each of their lives was so vast, so vibrant, so intricate in its infinite complexity. Just one was enough to lose himself, and there were thousands — hundreds of thousands — of past lives crowding his tired mind.

And past deaths, as well.

The cursed legionnaire had not perished on the day the sun rose above his fallen land. An eon of Corruption followed, spent in the embrace of frenzied agony. Just as he had predicted, the civilization built on the bones of a dreadful hecatomb was eventually destroyed, and all memories of his people were erased from the world. Only Corruption remained.

But the shadow remembered.

He remembered living myriad abominable lives under the starless abyss. During the day, a radiant sun flooded the world with brilliant light. At night, a dark sea drowned it with death and destruction. Revolting creatures dwelled in that desolate hell, and the shadow had been those creatures once.

He remembered living as the cursed soldiers of the fallen legion, devouring the corpses of the creatures the sea had killed. He remembered being monstrous centipedes that hid in the coral, waiting to ambush their prey and dissolve it in virulent acid. He remembered being ghastly spiders that wove webs made of razor-sharp steel. He remembered being flesh-eating flowers that bloomed in screaming bodies and wore them as shells. harrowing vines that sprawled for hundreds of meters under the mud, ensnaring those who were unfortunate enough to step on them and dragging them into the giant maw buried deep beneath. Colonies of loathsome termites that made their nests inside the corpses of dead leviathans and slowly devoured them from within.

He remembered being a towering tree that consumed souls by luring living things with the promise of sweet fruit, then stealing their minds to force them to guard, worship, and feed it.

Each of those ghastly lives was no less vast, vibrant, and intricate than the lives of three men he had remembered. They were like a mosaic. Put together, the disjointed fragments painted an all-encompassing picture of that terrifying, starless land.

The mental picture was so detailed that the shadow felt it could encompass that hellish realm, just like his senses encompassed the land around his cave. That he could fuse with it and dissolve in its endless horror, just like he did with the mortal realm that Tatal and her people had made their home. But why would he do that?

What good would fusing with a realm devoured by Corruption do? It would only allow Corruption to swallow him, as well. The shadow did not want to remember agony.

He only wanted peace.

But those memories had a pull that was hard to resist. Once he disturbed them with his careless thoughts, they took hold of his mind and refused to let go. And so, he drowned in them... he drowned, unable to break free...

“Shadow! Shadow!"

‘What the...'

The shadow was pulled from the ghastly sea of memories by an unreasonably loud, high-pitched voice. Dazed, he directed his gaze to the mouth of the cave and saw a familiar, tiny figure carefully making its way inside.

For a moment, he felt turned back.

‘Haven't I sent her back?'

He definitely had. And yet, here she was, demonstrably breaking the law of causality. Causality was one of the foundational laws of the universe. Not even the gods could impose on it easily... so how come the girl who was supposed to be somewhere else suddenly appeared in his cave?

There was no reasonable answer.

‘Did that old fool of a man decide to sacrifice her again?'

The only explanation the shadow could imagine was that somebody had brought the girl back. However, that didn't make much sense, either... after all, his warning was quite stark. The tribesmen would have to be complete fools to disregard it immediately.

But then again... the shadow’s sense of time was murky. He wasn't fully aware of how much of it had flown by since the moment he sent the girl back to her village. It felt like just a moment ago, but days seemed to have already passed.

"Uh-oh!"

Not at all aware of the inner turmoil that her appearance had caused the shadow, Tatal slid down the sloping entrance of the cave and clumsily fell to her knees.

“Ouchie..."

She did not, however, drop the oil lamp burning in her hand.

For the first time since the birth of the world, the shadow's shelter was illuminated by the radiance of fire. He was aghast, struggling to believe that somebody would be so bold as to bring a source of light into the vast darkness of his being.

‘What... is happening?’

Tatal, meanwhile, picked herself up from the stone, dusted off her crude garments, and glanced up with a grin.

"Shadow?"

The shadow hesitated.

Eventually, his voice resounded from the darkness.

"Yes?"

The girl's smile widened, and she waved at the darkness.

"I've come!"

That did not dispel his confusion one bit. He remained silent for a long while, digesting her statement and getting accustomed to a candle shining within the depths of his vast and formless being.

The light of the candle was feeble, of course. If the shadow wanted to, it could extinguish it with a thought — less than that, even. But then, Tatal would stumble in the dark... making all sorts of noises...

His peace and quiet were already gone, but there were degrees to this state of unrest. Wishing to avoid having to endure even more noise, the shadow let out a mental sigh and spared the little flame.

He lingered for a moment, then spoke.

"I see."

Then, after considering the situation a little more, the shadow asked:

“But why have you come?"

Tatal blinked a couple of times, staring into the darkness with an expression of sincere surprise.

Then, her grin returned.

“Because I thought that you'd be lonely!"

Her tone suggested that the answer should have been entirely obvious.

The shadow stared at her, utterly perplexed.

‘Aha.'

No one had brought the girl to the cave, and the law of causality had not been broken either. Instead, she was here of her own volition, having decided that the fearsome being that dwelled in the cave would be lonely there without her.

‘I shouldn't have expected a reasonable explanation. That was my mistake.'

There was some merit to Tatal's logic — he was alone in the cave, after all. It was just that her logic had nothing to do with reason...

It was little girl logic.

Since she would feel lonely living in a dark cave by herself, she assumed that Shadow would too.

Why was she concerned whether he was lonely or not, though?

The cold voice resounded from the darkness, sounding a little confused.

"Why would you care?"

Tatal tilted her head a little.

Then, she smiled.

“Because we're friends!"

The shadow was flabbergasted.

‘Since when?!’

He was sure that he would have noticed making a friend.

However, the girl sounded quite confident. There was no shadow of a doubt in her voice.

So, the shadow resolved to set her straight...

Somehow, though, he failed.

That was the first time the shadow had failed at anything since the dawn of time.

--- Chapter 3170 ---

"...This is my doll! Her name is Snuggle!"

Tatal showed the shadow the ugliest doll he had ever seen. It was made of coarse fabric and wore a crude dress that vaguely resembled Tatal's own. Two black beads served as its eyes, and its mouth seemed to be stuck in a perpetual frown.

Tatal was not the kind of girl to play with her toys gently, either. It looked like Snuggle had been torn countless times, then mended with clumsy stitches. As a result, she looked like a battle-hardened warrior covered in countless gruesome scars, not an innocent damsel's companion.

This was the first doll the shadow had ever seen — in this life, at least — and it was nearly unbearable to look at.

Still, Tatal seemed utterly in love with the ugly thing, so he kept his thoughts to himself.

"Say hi to Snuggle, Shadow!"

The girl grinned happily.

“What is your favorite berry, Shadow? Mine is raspberry. My second favorite is mulberry. But I like wild strawberry, blueberry, cranberry, and elderberry too! Oh, and winterberry. You'll get a tummy ache if you eat those, but they're pretty!"

The shadow had not known that there were this many types of berries. The only ones he knew were either poisonous or twisted by Corruption. So, he did not like berries much.

The shadow remained silent for a while. When he eventually spoke, his cold voice sounded a little strained...

"I don't like berries."

Tatal stared at the darkness, aghast.

She was scandalized.

"N—not... not even raspberries?"

The shadow had no idea what a raspberry was. Was that a berry that made your voice sound raspy if you ate it, or a berry that talked in a raspy voice? The former was strange, while the latter felt concerning.

He considered his answer for a long time...

“I can count to ten! Twenty, if I am not wearing shoes. How high can you count, Shadow?"

The shadow was not sure what shoes had to do with counting — in fact, he could not even imagine an answer. Still, he felt obligated to answer.

“As high as I want."

"Can you count to a hundred?"

"Yes."

“How about a thousand?"

"Yes."

“How about a ten thousand?"

"Yes."

"Wow!"

Tatal looked into the darkness with admiration. Then, her little face suddenly scrunched into an expression of grave suspicion, and after staying quiet for a few moments, she said somberly:

“Prove it, then. Count to ten thousand."

The shadow was baffled.

"What?"

"Then do it. You aren't lying to me, are you?" The shadow felt the desire to start an earthquake.

"I am not lying.”

"Then do it!"

"I won't."

"Ha! Liar!"

"l am not a liar... I am a very honest shadow. I haven't lied once since the dawn of time."

"Then do it!"

"I said I won't..."

Tatal's visits all went something like that. She came every once in a while after that first time, entirely ignoring the fact that the friend she had made was a disembodied mass of darkness that had dwelled in the ominous cave since the creation of the world.

The peace and quiet the shadow longed for were entirely obliterated. The antics of the carefree human child left him baffled, exasperated, and mentally exhausted every time. When his vast consciousness collided with Tatal's simple and impossibly straightforward worldview, unbelievably enough, it was the former that was left bruised and damaged.

The shadow had never wanted to be human, but as a result of Tatal unceremoniously invading his world, he could not help but feel more and more of her humanity leaving a mark on him.

That mark of humanity was not at all what the shadow enjoyed, let alone wanted.

But, at the same time...

He much preferred Tatal's company to that of all the other humans living in the settlement. Those who came to make offerings all wore strange garments and performed inexplicable rituals. They were full of a solemn sense of importance, fear, and reverence.

They treated the shadow as a fearsome deity... while not really understanding what a deity was.

The shadow disliked their worship much more than Tatal's complete lack of deference. In fact, her casual demeanor was not that unpleasant — unlike the veneration of the older members of her tribe.

Like that, time passed.

Seasons changed, and then changed again, killing the world and bringing it back to life once more. The shadow spent his time observing the lands surrounding his cave. He failed to reach the state of complete fusion with the world again, but it was still enough to bring his tired soul a sense of peace.

He remembered fragmented pieces of his past lives from time to time, as well, but he had never drowned in them again. His unwilling connection with Tatal prevented him from losing his sense of self too thoroughly, and as a result, it slowly grew firmer.

The human tribe, meanwhile, was developing swiftly. The forest retreated even further back, and their fields expanded. They were beginning to domesticate animals other than dogs and learning new crafts every day.

The Creatures of Corruption did not bother the tribe due to the presence of the shadow, and while they faced the hunger and fury of the beasts that populated the forest from time to time — both mundane and mythical — they had not faced anything powerful enough to wipe them out yet.

They had even established contact with several other human tribes dwelling in the neighboring lands. There was some tension between them, but overall, they all seemed to prefer trade and exchange over plundering and bloodshed.

More children were born, and the village grew.

The shadow observed the changing world indifferently.

"Shadow! Shadow!"

Once again, Tatal appeared at the mouth of his cave, smiling foolishly.

Only now, she wasn't a little girl anymore. In the blink of an eye, the tiny child had become a young woman on the cusp of adulthood. Her crude garments were replaced by a hunter's attire, and her ebony hair was gathered into a long braid, decorated tastefully with colorful beads and feathers.

She raised her bow triumphantly.

“Look what I caught!"

She was dragging the carcass of a massive cave bear behind her, straining her Awakened body to pull its crushing weight. The shadow stared at the giant bear — an Ascended Beast who had been terrorizing the tribe for a few decades now — in a state of mild amusement.

“Good job. But was there really a need to drag that thing here? Are you going to eat it?"

Dropping the paw of the cave bear, Tatal blinked a couple of times.

“Of course! The whole village will. Bear meat is not the tastiest, but you can make a stew. Its claws and teeth can be made into weapons. Its tendons will become bowstrings. The most important part is the hide, though!"

The shadow studied the bear. It seemed that Tatal had gone an extra mile not to damage the hideous beast's hide, even though hunting an Ascended creature must have been a deadly trial for a young Awakened woman like her.

He knew it had been, of course, because he had observed every moment of her hunt carefully.

The shadow was aware of everything that happened in his land, but he rarely paid it any attention. The ruckus Tatal had created was too much to ignore, though, so this time was an exception.

"What's so important about the hide?"

He was not really curious, but felt like he had to ask out of politeness.

Tatal grinned.

“I'll clean it and present it as a bridal gift to my fiancé!"

The shadow felt like his entire being froze. He did not have eyes, but if he did, one of them would have twitched.

“Your what?"

Tatal seemed surprised. She stared at the darkness, blinked a couple of times, and then giggled.

"What, you didn't know? I'm getting married!"

The shadow had not, indeed, known. Perhaps he should have paid more attention.

--- Chapter 3171 ---

Tatal's wedding was a grand affair...

By the standards of the nascent civilization of the Age of Gods, naturally.

The whole village participated in the preparations. The best seamstress of the tribe prepared her wedding dress; the hunters ventured deep into the forest to procure meat for the feast. A few of the daring youths robbed the nest of an Awakened queen bee and made it away with several jars of mystical honey.

The shadow had to scare the enraged creature into abandoning its plans of revenge.

The old women created an elaborate headdress, using ember, carnelian, and rubies to decorate it. An elderly craftsman carved the auspicious charm — the figurine of a ferocious wolf — from a piece of precious jade.

Special dyes were created. The shaman of a tribe spent many days preparing to officiate the ritual. The children prowled the forest, searching for sweet berries on the ground and glistening gemstones in the streams.

Usually, the tribesmen would build a home for the newlywed couple. But ever since Tatal's grandfather passed away several years ago, she had lived alone in his house — one of the largest in the village, decorated with bestial skulls and fearsome antlers.

The shadow was surprised by how much work went into ensuring that Tatal's wedding was as grand and festive as possible. Granted, she was not just any young girl — despite her youth, Tatal was special to the tribe. She was the last descendant of its most fearsome hunter, after all, and a powerful Awakened in her own right.

She had been very young when she Awakened, too — unusually so — and powerful as well. So, the elders treasured Tatal, hoping that she would grow more powerful in the future... perhaps even more powerful than her grandfather had been, and would therefore ensure the safety and prosperity of the tribe once they were gone.

And, naturally, there was the fact that she had been offered as a sacrifice to the terrifying creature that dwelled in the darkness, and was returned to the tribe alive.

So, perhaps it was no surprise that the tribe treated her wedding with such zeal. In fact, it had taken a lot to arrange the marriage itself.

By then, it was customary for the young people of neighboring tribes to marry each other. The chieftain of the tribe — its best hunter — was usually a man, while the shaman was usually a woman. The former dealt with outside threats, while the latter took care of the people, so women held more authority in the inner workings of a tribe. Therefore, the groom usually moved to live with the bride's family.

However, Tatal was not just anyone — sadly, there were no suitable young men in the neighboring tribes to become her husband. So, the elders put a lot of effort into reaching out to the far reaches of the realm, eventually finding her an outstanding groom among the youths of the Grey Wolf Tribe — a tribe of fearsome hunters that had yet to abandon its nomadic ways, wandering the vast expanse of the realm despite its many dangers.

While learning about the Grey Wolf Tribe, the shadow was also surprised to learn how Tatal's own tribe was called...

It was the Shadow Tribe.

And the reason her people were called that was none other than the shadow himself, even if he had known nothing about it.

It seemed that all tribes of humans came from a small number of great tribes who had formed a long time ago, when their ancestors left the blissful cradle of the Heart Forest.

As they spread over the mortal realms and their numbers increased, the tribes splintered — when the number of people outgrew the ability of the land to support them, someone had to leave in search of a different route in untamed wilderness. That was how humans swiftly settled most of the mortal realms, and when there was nowhere else to go, they had no choice but to settle and invent agriculture to sustain their growing population. And that, in turn, was how the shadow had ended up with his noisy, frustrating neighbors.

The ancient, great tribes were each called by the name of the guardian Spirit they worshipped. The tribe guarded by the fearsome Sacred beast, the Wolf, was called the Wolf Tribe, for example — its smaller offshoots would add an epithet to their name, one for each degree of separation from their guardian Spirit. Some of the youngest tribes would not have any name at all, having lost the connection to their deity.

That meant that the Grey Wolf tribe was old and powerful, having proven its ability to survive across dozens of generations. The Shadow Tribe, however, only had one word in its name, since there was no other group of humans protected by the shadow — it was the first of its kind.

That made its status ambiguous, so the elders had outdone themselves to secure Tatal a promising youth of the Grey Wolves. The shadow really couldn't complain.

He still wanted to, though.

‘What is she thinking about? Marriage? Too young! She's too young!’

He found himself experiencing a lot of emotions he could not quite explain. The shadow rarely felt anything that could be rightfully described as emotion, really, so it was no surprise that he could not discern his own feeling, let alone where they came from.

The greater surprise was that he felt anything at all.

Tatal... seemed happy, though, so he couldn't say anything. He wasn't entirely unhappy about whom the elders had chosen for her, either.

The Wolf. That name resonated with him, because he had been the Wolf once.

Which meant that he had killed it once, as well.

The descendants of the people who had forged a bond with the Spirit Wolf could not be terrible people. They had to be strong, at least — far stronger than Tatal's own people were.

Besides that, wolves were pack animals. They knew the value of family. So, the shadow believed that Tatal's future husband would treat her well.

And if not...

Well then, the shadow had killed the guardian Spirit of those people. Dealing with a mortal pup would be as easy as looking his way.

‘At least they had the sense to arrange a marriage with a Wolf Tribe.’

If it had been a tribe worshipping an unworthy beast, the shadow would not have stayed quiet. In fact, he would have had to put his foot down...

The shadow did not really have a foot, but the point still stood.

--- Chapter 3172 ---

The wedding came and went.

It was a splendid affair... that was what a human would have said, at least. To the shadow, it seemed like more of the strange behavior the tribesmen showcased when leaving him offerings at the mouth of the cave.

There were solemn movements. There was incoherent mumbling. The elderly shaman performed a dance... she was surprisingly energetic for a woman of her age, but somehow still retained enough stamina to offer devotions to the crude statues of the six great gods that stood in the village's small shrine.

Tatal, at least, looked beautiful in her wedding attire. With amber and carnelian sewn into the fabric and decorating her hair, she seemed like a flame... a small flame, no different from the candle she had held when visiting the shadow in his cave for the first time.

The groom... was not bad, no matter how much it pained the shadow to admit it. The youth seemed glum for a while, but after seeing Tatal for the first time, his eyes ignited with a silly kind of fervor. That mesmerized glint told the shadow that the two human children would, perhaps, be alright.

A few days after the wedding, Tatal came to his cave in high spirits.

"Shadow!"

She called the shadow out each time, even though his vast darkness encompassed the entire cave, and he never left.

The shadow studied the young woman for a moment. Confirming that she was in a good mood, he asked in his usual cold tone:

“What?"

She beamed.

"Well? Did you see him? Isn't he tall? Isn't he handsome?"

The shadow had no sense to distinguish a handsome human from a dull one, but the boy from the Grey Wold tribe was indeed tall.

‘What's the big deal about being tall, anyway?’

The shadow was inexplicably displeased.

"I saw."

He did not offer further commentary.

Tatal laughed boisterously.

“My husband is the most handsome man in the tribe! No, in the neighboring tribes as well! Even though he doesn't have a beard yet... ah, but I am sure it will grow eventually!"

The shadow sighed.

“You humans are certainly fond of hair."

Tatal gave the darkness a pitying look.

“Of course. What kind of man doesn't have a beard? Let me tell you... my grandfather's beard was the thickest in the tribe. That was why he was the manliest."

The shadow felt like there was something wrong with that statement, but what did he know?

He didn't have a beard, either, and he wasn't really a man — he was a disembodied shadow. There was some kind of causality between the two facts, and he wasn't going to bother discerning what it was.

What he was sure of, however, was that men without beards were far more handsome and dashing. The shadow did not know where that confident opinion came from, but felt that he was right.

“I brought you hawthorn wine. Do you know what wine is, Shadow? The Grey Wolf people brought it with them. It's delicious!"

Tatal produced a gourd and offered it to the darkness. The shadow stared at the gourd dubiously for a few moments, then answered in an indifferent tone:

"I do know what wine is. However, I won't drink it."

Tatal grinned.

"Oh, no. What a pity. We can't let this wine go to waste, though, can we?"

With that, she retracted the ground and drank from it with a satisfied expression.

‘This vixen...'

Tatal knew perfectly well that the shadow did not eat or drink. In fact, she knew it so well that she had been secretly stuffing herself with the offerings the villagers left on his altar ever since she was a little girl. The shadow wasn't going to eat them, and the little glutton saw no reason to let all those sweet things go to waste.

Satisfied with the wine, Tatal looked around.

"Anyway... this marriage thing. It's great!"

She scratched the back of her head.

“Have you ever been married, Shadow?"

As Tatal took another gulp of the wine, the shadow gave her an unamused look.

Then, he answered honestly:

“Many times."

He had lived hundreds of thousands of lives, after all.

Tatal spat out the wine.

"W—what?"

Her voice trembled.

"What do you mean, many times? That's not allowed, Shadow! You can only marry one person, for life!"

The shadow answered in an emotionless tone:

"If you're human."

Tatal stared at the darkness, then scoffed.

"When would you even have time to get married? You never leave your cave! You're lying again."

At that moment, the shadow did something he had never done before — in this lifetime, at least.

He chuckled.

His voice sounded a little amused when he spoke:

“You're right. I have no time to get married."

As he said that, though, he seemed to remember something.

A beautiful radiance. A reflection of white flames dancing in someone's eyes. A soothing warmth permeating his entire being...

An almost unbearable sense of longing.

The shadow was confused.

Why would a shadow like him long for light?

It didn't make any sense.

Just like Tatal and other humans never made sense.

He remained silent for a long while, then said quietly:

“Congratulations on your marriage, Tatal. I am glad that the groom is to your liking.”

She smiled.

“Thank you. I am glad too."

After taking another gulp of the wine, she added:

“Makes me feel like hunting that damn bear was worth it!"

The sound of her laughter filled the cave. The shadow noticed that, somehow, he wasn't irritated by that noise anymore.

Soon, having finished the wine and gushed about her new husband enough, Tatal returned to her tribe, leaving him alone in silence.

The shadow remained motionless, quiet.

In his mind...

The reflections of the white flame were still dancing, filling his chest with an indescribable ache.

Then, however, he dispelled that strange state and settled into his usual position. Watching, waiting.

Knowing that there was nothing to wait for, and that he had already seen far too much.

--- Chapter 3173 ---

The world moved on.

Tatal settled into her married life, and the shadow settled into his usual aloof existence. He felt the land around him change slowly. The trees reached desperately for the sky. the beasts prowled the forest, hunting those who were weaker than them while being hunted by those who were stronger.

Tatal became much busier as she matured and built her family. Her young husband proved to be a hunter of great skill and talent, effortlessly demonstrating his worth to the men of the Shadow Tribe and eventually becoming their leader. The old shaman who had officiated the wedding, meanwhile, was beginning to succumb to her age.

As a result, it was decided that Tatal would become her successor. She began her training not long after the wedding, and it consumed most of her time.

Her visits to the dark cave where the shadow dwelled slowly grew less frequent. Still, she made an effort to come at least once a month, bringing news of the outside world and chatting with him about nonsensical things that only a human could find engaging.

Then, the number of her visits reduced to once every few months or when something important happened.

That was because Tatal was with child.

Soon enough, she came to the dark cave carrying a small bundle of cloth. Nestled within the bundle was a tiny infant, its face red and wrinkly.

Tatal's own face shone with a subtle light that the shadow had not seen before, and a soft, unfamiliar smile played on her lips.

"Look, Shadow."

She presented the bundle to the darkness, then gently pressed it to her chest.

"This is my son. Isn't he lovely?"

To the shadow, the infant looked like a strangely shaped lump of uncooked dough — ugly, to say the least. Even Snuggle had more charm than it.

However, inexplicably, he could not help but feel that the tiny human was, indeed, lovely. It was so lovely that the shadow could not express it with words.

Perhaps because the infant was a part of Tatal.

Eventually, his cold voice resounded from the darkness.

“Yes. He is beautiful.”

After becoming a mother and assuming some of the duties from the faltering old shaman, Tatal rarely had time to escape all her responsibilities and venture into the mountains to visit her reclusive friend. However, she still came once a year, every year — on the day they had first met.

The world was slowly changing. The village expanded, the forest around it replaced by fields. A master from a neighboring tribe came to build a crude stone mill. The humans learned something new every month, swiftly developing in all manner of crafts.

One year, Tatal brought with her a sharp blade. She showed it to the shadow, full of reverence.

“Look, Shadow. This is called copper. It comes from the earth, like stone... however, unlike flint, it never breaks. It never chips, never crumbles. It can pierce the toughest hide while remaining whole. Is it not a miracle?"

Even though Tatal was performing the role of a shaman now, in her heart, she was still a hunter. So, her eyes shone with wonder as she looked at the copper knife.

Another time, Tatal brought a pile of bricks. Her voice sounded excited.

“Look, Shadow! This is called clay. I saw it when I visited the Crow Tribe — their chieftain's home is built from these things. He called them bricks. And you can get clay easily, too! My husband has been digging clay for a week now. I told him that if that haughty Crow has a brick home, then we must have one, too!"

And yet another time, the shadow was disturbed by the sound of panicked bleating and saw Tatal dragging a skinny sheep with a red coat into the cave, holding it by the horns.

"Shadow! Shadow, look!"

The shadow felt the desire to palm his face, even though he had none.

‘Gods, what is it now?’

“What is that... thing?"

Tatal smiled.

“It's called a sheep! My grandfather used to hunt these beasts for meat and hide. However... they shed their coats every year. So, if you look after them a little, you can weave as much cloth as you want. Wool, Shadow! Don't you see my dress? It's so much lighter than hide — and softer, too. No one else in the village has one yet!"

She paused for a moment, and then laughed ominously.

“Those arrogant Crows will die of envy the next time we meet."

The shadow... was impressed.

Tatal's people seemed to be developing faster than he had expected. Perhaps it was because War God, the goddess of life — as well as technology and progress — was the divine patron of all humans. Maybe it was because they were descendants of the First Humans, who had wielded mythical power and had been creatures of myriad talents.

But, of course, not all of Tatal's visits were happy ones.

Life was a constant struggle, after all, and it was especially so for the ancient people who lived in the Age of Gods.

The shadow's presence might have scared off most of the Creatures of Corruption, but there were still some who failed to perceive him or were too mad to be turned away. There was no peace between humans and mystical beasts that dwelled in the untamed expanse of existence, either.

Even mundane predators were a deadly threat to them, at times, fighting desperately for ownership over the wild land.

There were other human tribes, as well. There was famine and disease. There was the unpredictable harshness of indifferent nature. The life of Tatal and her tribe was idyllic at times, while at times it was full of strife, struggle, and sorrow.

And even if Tatal did not show it, the shadow knew that she felt the harshness of the world more deeply than most. She had been orphaned at a young age, after all, and then thrown into a dark cave to die by the person whom she trusted the most. Her heart had been wounded, and so it was more sensitive to pain.

Tatal was still young when the old shaman died, and she became the new one. The responsibility over the entire tribe suddenly fell onto her shoulders, and when she appeared at the mouth of the shadow's cave — far ahead of her usual visit — there was fear and uncertainty written on her pale, tired face.

"I don't know, Shadow... I don't know what to do. Human life is so fragile. One wrong decision — less than that, even, just a bit of bad luck — and the entire tribe will be gone. It's terrifying. The elders shield themselves from that terror with blind faith... faith in the gods, faith that tomorrow will be the same as today... but I cannot be like them. I wish that I could."

She looked deeply troubled. The shadow tried to console her as best he could, but he was not someone who knew solace well. His own existence was endless and endlessly arduous, after all. There was no solace to be found for him, so how could he soothe another?

Tatal came to him after her second daughter died of fever, as well. This time, she didn't say anything, and just sat silently in the darkness, tears streaming down her face. The shadow did not try to console her, since she was inconsolable. He simply stayed by her side, all around her, allowing his darkness to hide her tears from the world.

Another year, a man of her tribe killed another in a fit of jealousy. Conflict was commonplace among the people of the tribe, but crime was rare. Its people stood together against the hostile world, after all — they had to trust and support each other in order to survive. A tribe could only survive in unity, and since crime undermined it, those who broke the unspoken laws and customs were dealt with harshly.

Thieves, murderers, and people who used force to get what they want — there was no place for them among the people of the tribe.

The criminals were meant to be banished... but, actually, banishment was considered to be the cruelest of punishments. If the shaman was merciful, she would sentence the guilty to death instead.

Tatal was one such shaman. Usually, the chieftain of the tribe — the strongest of the hunters — would carry out the execution. But since Tatal was stronger than the strongest among the tribe's warriors, or perhaps for some other reason, she chose to end the murderer's life with her own hands. She came to the shadow's cave a few days after that, surrounded by a somber silence. Her face was motionless, and her gaze was distant. There was a painful, burdened ache in its depths.

After sitting silently on the stone floor for a long while, she spoke quietly.

"I've never killed a human before, Shadow."

Her voice was heavy, as if pressed down by crushing weight.

Tatal took a breath, then sighed.

"I never thought I would."

She smiled joylessly, then looked into the darkness.

"Have you ever killed a person, Shadow?"

His cold voice resounded in the cave, as calm and unaffected as it had always been.

"Too countless to count."

Tatal's lips trembled.

She studied the darkness with a pained expression, and then asked in a fragile tone:

"How do you live?"

The shadow remained silent for a short while.

Eventually, having failed to find a better answer, he answered simply:

"One day at a time."

Tatal stared at the darkness.

Slowly, her pale smile brightened a little, as if she was amused by something.

Looking down, she laughed quietly and whispered.

"One day at a time..."

Life went on. Tatal seemed to have found the courage to face it again, meeting its countless challenges one at a time — and overcoming them.

Her tribe overcame all the adversity that the world threw at it, as well.

They survived. They grew.

They flourished.

It was funny... the shadow had witnessed great and terrible beings fighting each other across the vast expanse of the newborn world. He had beheld gods and demons — albeit from afar. He had felt the earth trembling under their footsteps and seen them reshape all of existence with their dire feats.

But, somehow, the mundane and fleeting lives of the small, insignificant people of the tribe had become far more fascinating and meaningful to him, at some point.

Because Tatal was one of them.

Time passed, and she turned from a young girl into a woman who carried the weight of her duty and responsibility with grace. Despite the scars left on her heart, she was still full of joy and resolve. She enjoyed all the boons that life had to offer — fully and never holding anything back.

However, life had no shortage of ordeals in store for those who dared to face it with a smile.

And so, soon enough, Tatal's harshest trial yet arrived.

--- Chapter 3174 ---

Tatal was an Ascended by then, having lived up to the expectations of the tribe's elders and become as powerful as her grandfather had been at the peak of his power. She had learned how to be a warrior from him. The previous shaman, meanwhile, had taught her the secret of sorcery, making her a Shaper.

Most of those elders had already left for the Realm of Shadows by then, and those who still lived were too old and decrepit to manage the affairs of the tribe. So, the responsibility for its well-being lay squarely on Tatal's shoulders. She did her best to safeguard her people — but, just as she had mentioned once, disaster was always around the corner.

Sometimes, it took less than a single bad decision to doom a tribe of humans. All that stood between them and extinction was a bit of bad luck.

This time, the bad luck of Tatal's people came from far away.

North of their valley, deep in the primal forest, lived the tribe of the One-Winged Crow. And beyond that, on the shore of a wide river, lived the tribe of the Sabertooth Tiger — they were the ones who brought calamity upon the people of this distant land.

No one knew how it happened, but the people of that tribe had somehow earned the wrath of a powerful Transcendent creature that dwelled in the heart of a vast and deadly marsh. Perhaps they had offended it somehow, or perhaps they had simply disturbed its slumber...

Perhaps the creature needed no reason at all, and was simply incensed by the smell of humans.

That creature was the Basilisk, and before anyone knew it, the Sabertooth tribe was entirely wiped out.

The shadow was not just anyone, of course. He knew it all because the den of the Basilisk was well within the borders of the vast area encompassed by its senses.

But what did he care if some tribe was destroyed by an enraged Devil? The Basilisk was not a Creature of Corruption, after all, and those people had brought its wrath upon themselves.

There was no peace among humans and noble creatures that populated the world. So what if all of them had come from the Flame? They still competed for the same forests, plains, and lakes. Some creatures built a relationship with humans, but some saw them as hateful pests instead. Some simply treated them as all other living beings — the weak were prey, the strong were a threat.

That Basilisk had been slumbering in the marsh for centuries, patiently incubating a clutch of precious eggs. The crafty humans thought that they could steal the eggs without awakening the giant creature, but panicked and destroyed them instead.

So, the shadow saw no reason to intervene... he did not care to intervene even if there had been a reason. Bullying a little Transcendent wyrm was not a good look for beings like him, anyway.

The problem, however, was that the Basilisk did not stop after destroying the Sabertooth tribe. Its rampage continued unabated, as if it was determined to eradicate all humans, everywhere, and soon, the neighboring tribes had tasted its wrath as well.

News spread slowly among the ancient humans, so most of them died without knowing the reason why their lives had come to an end. Entire villages were wiped out... the forest burned.

It was only when pillars of smoke rose into the sky, and battered refugees reached the surrounding tribes, their glassy eyes full of terror, that people learned about the approaching calamity.

But, for most of them, it was already too late.

That Shadow Tribe was late to learn the news, as well. In fact, they only learned it after tragedy struck.

When a handful of surviving Crows stumbled into their village — the last of the destroyed tribe — and told their tale in quiet, trembling voices, the first thing Tatal did was turn to look at the forest.

That was because her husband had led his men on a hunt a few days ago, venturing in the exact direction where the Basilisk was prowling.

Nobody knew if the hunters would return alive.

In the end... only a few of them did.

The hunting party had encountered the giant wyrm in the depths of the forest, and despite their courage and quick reflexes, the battle was brutal and one-sided. Most of them perished in a matter of moments,

and those who survived were only alive because of their chieftain's swift thinking, composure, and personal valor.

The chieftain himself — the little Wolf who had married Tatal once — returned alive, as well. However, he was grievously wounded. Worse than that, most of his right arm had turned to stone.

It was apparent that he would never hunt again.

The loss of the hunters and the crippling wounds of its chieftain were already a terrible blow for the tribe. But that was not where their problem ended — the Basilisk was still full of wrath and bloodlust, after all, and if it had already come this close to the village, it was only a matter of time before it descended upon it.

A world-ending disaster seemed to have befallen Tatal and her people.

The survivors of the Crow tribe, who had seen the Basilisk destroy their settlement like a living calamity, had only one piece of advice — run.

Run away, and pray to the gods for mercy. However, Tatal was in no hurry to flee with her people.

Looking at the village with a somber expression, she saw what others failed or refused to see.

There were too many people in the tribe now. They could abandon their homes and their livelihoods, but not all of them would survive away from their land — many would starve or die from exposure. Perhaps even most of them.

The land was a generous mother that fed and clothed them, but it was also a trap that tied them down like an inescapable shackle.

Even if they did survive... there was nowhere else to go.

After all, there was a reason why the elders had been forced to settle down. The land was vast, but it was not boundless. Every place where humans could survive had already been claimed by older and more powerful tribes, and those tribes would not welcome a crowd of hungry strangers — life was harsh for everyone, after all, and they were struggling to sustain their own people. So, if Tatal chose to take her people and flee, they would have only two ways to survive.

One would be for the tribe to disband, its people scattering to look for new homes. A few would be accepted by this village, a few would be accepted by that one... some would not be accepted at all. Most would perish in the wilderness, trying to make their way to a human settlement, and many of those who survived would spend the rest of their lives being treated badly by the original members of their new tribes.

The other way was simpler.

It was to take the land from another tribe, slaughtering its people and taking their place.

Things like that happened often. This realm was too remote and sparsely populated, and most of the tribes populating it were young, having only settled recently. But in the places that the Shadow Tribe had come from, humans turned their weapons against each other often... that was what the elders said, at least, since the oldest of them had witnessed it personally.

But even if Tatal was willing to take another tribe's land by force, there was no point in trying. She wouldn't do it, anyway.

Looking at the people of the Crow tribe, whose faces were pale like those of corpses, she said in a dark tone:

“Run? Can you outrun a Transcendent beast? How fast are you going to run, fools?"

If the beast was determined to eradicate all humans in the land, trying to run away would not save anyone.

The people looked at her in despair.

Several tribes were already gone. The Shadow Tribe seemed like it would follow them soon. Only gods knew how many more would be wiped out before the beast's fury was satiated, or before a more powerful creature stopped its rampage. They couldn't even flee.

Such was the fate of humans in the age when gods and daemons walked the earth. They were like ants beneath the feet of great and terrible beings... the horror of such existence could only be endured by turning yourself blind to the truth of the world.

But when the truth came knocking on your door, shutting your eyes was useless.

Tatal looked at the healer's house, where her husband was being treated. She looked at her frightened people. Then, she looked at the vast, dark forest beyond the fields.

"So what do we do, shaman? How can we survive?"

She remained silent for a long while, then unsheathed her precious copper knife and lowered her gaze to its sharp, polished blade.

At that point, the shadow expected her to pay his cave a visit.

But, to his surprise and dismay, Tatal went in the opposite direction instead.

Taking her bow and her spear, she changed from her beautifully embroidered wool dress into hide and leather, then left the village alone and entered the forest. She walked in the direction where the tribe's huntsmen had died.

‘What is that child doing?'

The shadow stirred, frowning mentally.

‘Has she lost her mind?’

Tatal did not seem panicked or grief-stricken. Her expression was somber, but also calm.

Her eyes were full of sorrow, but also dark and unshaken resolve.

‘Where are you going, fool?’

The shadow gnashed its teeth — he would have, rather, if he had them. The vast darkness of his being seethed restlessly. But, oblivious to his inner turmoil, Tatal continued moving toward danger.

By the morning of the next day, she reached the spot where the Basilisk had attacked the hunters. There, paling at the sight of carnage, she gritted her teeth and began tracking the beast.

It was then that the shadow did something he had not done in countless years... that he had never wanted or thought to do since the birth of the world.

He left his cave, manifesting into a vaguely human shape in Tatal's path.

His cold voice was stern when he asked, barely suppressing his irritation:

"What do you think you're doing?"

Tatal looked at him in confusion, then smiled faintly.

"Shadow?"

She hesitated for a moment, then continued walking, soon passing him.

“I'm on my way to kill the Basilisk. What else?"

Tatal inhaled deeply, then said in a lighthearted tone:

"My husband will be down when he comes to his senses and finds out what happened to his arm. So... I'll bring him the Basilisk's hide as a present. It won't be as soft as bear hide, but it might still lift his mood."

The shadow pursed his lips, then spun around and followed.

“Foolish girl, you have barely Ascended. That wyrm is a Transcendent Devil... it was one step away from becoming a Tyrant. Why are you trying to fight it? Why are you here alone?"

Tatal shrugged.

"You said it yourself, Shadow. The beast is Transcendent... those of my warriors that still live are no more than Awakened. Their spears won't even scratch its scales."

The shadow almost cursed.

"Isn't there someone else who can help you?"

Tatal raised an eyebrow.

"I can pray to the gods, I guess. But the gods are too great and distant to care about a mortal woman like me. So I'd rather not waste my breath."

This time, the shadow did have teeth. So, he gritted them and fell silent for a short while, trying to suppress the words that struggled to escape his mouth.

But, in the end, he couldn't — even if his entire being rose against uttering them aloud.

“Me! You could have asked me! That little worm is nothing for me! I can kill it in a second!"

Tatal continued walking, a pale smile illuminating her face.

In the end, she shook her head quietly.

“No, Shadow. I could never ask you to kill someone for me."

He scoffed.

“Why?"

Tatal lowered her head.

After taking half a dozen steps, she turned to look at him, a deep emotion hidden in her eyes.

"I think I understand now, Shadow... the reason you refused to kill me, all those years ago."

Tatal looked ahead.

"I have only ever killed one person, and the burden of that death is still following me around. But you, you said that you had killed too many living things to count. That weight... it must be crushing you, Shadow. How could I ever ask you to kill more? For me?"

She smiled sadly.

“What kind of friend would ask that?"

The shadow stared at her, aghast.

That foolish, little human... was pitying him? Was concerned about him?

‘Humans really are the silliest of creatures!’

He exhaled slowly.

“So you'd rather put your entire tribe in danger? Your husband? You children? You'd rather risk... yourself?"

Tatal remained silent for a long while. When she looked at the shadow again, her smile was gone, replaced by a soft expression.

"Shadow... I'm not that selfless, Shadow."

She shook her head slowly.

"It's just that even if all of them have forgotten — and you as well, perhaps — I still remember. I realized it at some point, years ago."

She smiled at him.

"You are the greatest danger to my tribe, Shadow. We are alive only because you allow us to live. If you can kill the Basilisk in a second, then how long will it take you to wipe us out? How easy would it be for you to kill us all?"

She pursed his lips.

"This calamity has happened because the Basilisk started killing and couldn't stop. What happens if you start killing on my behalf? Will there come a day when you won't stop?"

Her voice grew quieter.

“Will there come a day when I won't be able to stop myself from asking you to kill for me?"

Looking down, Tatal shook her head.

“No... that man I killed. I sentenced him to death, so I took his life with my own hands, without asking someone else to bloody theirs. The Basilisk is no different. I have decided that its life must end, so I will end it!"

With that, she hurried her steps.

The shadow fell back, watching her go in stunned silence.

At that moment, he felt something he had not felt in a long while... had never felt before, perhaps.

The familiar, biting sting of powerlessness.

...A few days later, after a long and dreadful battle, surrounded by shattered cliffs and ravaged earth, Tatal slayed a Transcendent Devil, the Basilisk, with her copper blade. She ended its life with her own hands, without asking anyone else to do it for her.

She could not take its hide to gift it to her husband, though, because it was as tough as stone — the copper knife was utterly powerless against it. So, the shadow helped her skin the dead Devil.

--- Chapter 3175 ---

Tatal had been gravely wounded in the battle against the Basilisk. In fact, she was barely alive.

But she was alive.

The shadow delivered her unconscious body, as well as the hide of the slain Devil, to the outskirts of the village. Then, he disappeared and returned to the comfortable, cold darkness of his cave. The tribesmen had to be full of shock and joy at the return of their shaman. After all, slaying the Basilisk was not what a mere Ascended was meant to be capable of... the battle Tatal had fought was, without a doubt, a spectacular and awesome feat — a feat worthy of becoming a song, or perhaps even a myth, one day.

The myth of a valiant shaman who faced an unstoppable calamity with a song and a copper blade.

But the shadow was in no mood to observe the tribesmen celebrating.

He was troubled... he was uneasy.

Even now that the Basilisk was dead and Tatal was out of danger, the shadow still felt strangely disturbed. It was all because of what Tatal had said, back in the depths of the forest.

‘Why did she refuse my help?’
