The shadow was like a god to the people of the small human tribe. So why would Tatal turn away from her god and choose to face the Devil alone?

The shadow did not know why, but that question resonated with the depths of his dark being.

A fragment of a long-forgotten conversation surfaced from the depths of his mind, spoken by a man he did not remember in a life he did not want to recall.

‘Never trust the gods...’

Who had said it?

What did it mean?

The shadow already knew the kind of chilling horror lesser creatures felt when faced with the unfathomable vastness of Divine and Unholy beings — and of those who were Sacred or Cursed, as well. Being so small, so insignificant, so indescribably powerless... it almost made everything feel meaningless.

The only way to keep your sanity while sharing a world with such beings was not to think about their greatness at all.

However, the shadow had only ever considered the gods as a harrowing, inescapable threat. They did not even need to harbor any hostility against the shadow to destroy him. Entire realms could perish from the smallest aftershock of their actions — in front of them, even a being like him was no more than an ant, and just like an ant, he could be crushed by the careless steps of these giants.

He had only ever thought about the gods as an odd, inherently hazardous and calamitous force. He always assumed that beings that were lesser than him, like the tribesmen, would feel the same way.

But what if a god was benevolent, instead? What if a god was gentle and cared about you? What if they were willing to extend a helping hand without asking anything in return?

One would assume that having a god's favor would be an incredible boon. Who had not hoped for a miracle, after all? Who had not wished for there to be an all-powerful, kind being watching over them?

The shadow was neither kind nor all-powerful, but he could have been Tatal’s miracle.

And yet, she had refused him. It was for his benefit, yes, since she considered him a dear friend. But it was for her own benefit as well — her words hinted at that, implying something he had never considered

before...

That a benevolent god was just as terrifying as a hostile one — maybe even more so.

‘Why?’

The shadow spent a long time in the darkness, thinking.

In the end, he came to a conclusion that made him uncomfortable. That conclusion was not about what Tatal believed, but rather about what the shadow himself felt would be true... but that did not make it any less confusing.

It was that the existence of a kind god still rendered the efforts of mortals meaningless, while their benevolence was too sweet to resist — once someone tasted it, there was no going back.

If the great gods existed and were willing to pay attention to the lives of mortals, then what were mortals to do? They could strive to accomplish something for their entire lives, and in the end, everything they achieved would still be infinitely inferior to a deity's casual act. Their lives would feel fleeting and dreary, pathetic and pitiful in comparison to the glorious existence of gods.

They would only be able to look in envy at what gods could do, what gods created, and what gods possessed.

Power, freedom, abundance, immortality... Life was harsh, and mortals could endure its harshness because that was the reality that all living things had to confront. But what if they had to behold beings who were unbound by reality, who treated reality as soft and malleable instead?

That, the shadow surmised, would fill them with a heartbreaking sense of injustice.

Of maddening envy and quiet despair. Faced with the greatness of gods, mortals would only have two choices. One was to continue living their lives, heartbroken, while the other was to throw themselves on the perilous Path of Ascension in hopes of becoming a deity one day, too.

But that was just one side of the coin.

On the other side was the danger of receiving help from a deity.

Humans were small and weak, but gods were great and all-powerful. So, what if a god descended into a mortal realm to help its people?

Once a deity helped them once, wouldn't they want to receive that help once more? And if they continued to be favored by their god, wouldn't they come to expect divine assistance? Wouldn't they come to rely on it, forgetting their own efforts?

What would happen if a deity solved all their problems, protected them from all the dangers, and gave them all the things they desired?

The shadow remembered the awe Tatal had felt when she saw copper for the first time, and the joy she shared with him when the craftsmen of her tribe learned to work it. The enthusiasm she was brimming with when figuring out how to make clay bricks. The boastful pride she was full of because of her wool dress — the first one in the village.

He knew that he could have created her a blade that was a thousand times more durable than copper with a thought. He could build a city for her tribe in a matter of minutes. He could weave a fabric that was more sublime and wondrous than anything Tatal had ever worn, touched, and seen.

He could have killed the Basilisk, as well. But if he had... would Tatal ever be able to overcome the temptation of asking him for more?

Of killing more of her enemies. Of providing more for her tribe. Of making life less harsh... of overcoming the struggles of life in her stead.

And if that happened, then would her joy, enthusiasm, and pride disappear one day? Would they be extinguished, little by little, like a flame starving without fuel?

Stolen away by the generous deity.

The shadow stirred.

It did not know.

It felt like Tatal had fathomed something that even he, a being far greater and more ancient than her, had not.

That it was hazardous for mortals to be subjects of divine affection.

Countless people across history had not felt the same. The two men of the Empire he remembered were certainly comfortable serving a nation ruled directly by a god.

But then again, was the Empire really the best example? Or was it exactly the kind of malignant anomaly that Tatal was reluctant to create?

The great and glorious Empire of War,

which conquered the world with fire and sword... whose conquest could not be resisted or stopped, because it was protected by a god.

Until, one day, it was stopped. The people who stopped it simply had to kill the gods first, destroying all of existence with them. The shadow rested in the darkness, uncomfortable. He did not know why the issue of godhood concerned him so much, let alone the issue of the relationship between gods and people.

He wasn't a god, after all, and neither did he have the desire to help people.

Tatal was the singular exception to his indifferent attitude toward all humans, and since she did not want his help, the point was moot.

So, the shadow could forget all about it and rest easily, knowing that these maddening questions had nothing to do with him.

--- Chapter 3176 ---

Tatal eventually recovered from her wounds.

Her tribe had not been forced to abandon its land and scatter to the winds.

Instead, it absorbed the survivors of the Basilisk's rampage and grew. Its reputation had soared, as well, since people of the surrounding lands — those lucky enough to have been spared the Devil's wrath — eventually learned that it was Tatal, the shaman of the Shadow Tribe, who had slain the beast.

There were hard times, at first, because the hunters of the tribe had been decimated, and its chieftain had lost an arm. But the tribe survived and grew stronger for it. The Basilisk had given it great boons in death. Its hide, its bones, its fangs, its soul shards — all of it was used by the tribesmen to empower themselves.

Soon enough, the youths reached adulthood. Trained by Stone Hand, their former chieftain, they became skilled hunters and replaced those who had perished in the woods. The fields expanded. The craftsmen of the tribe developed their craft and reached new heights.

Tatal ruled wisely. She was both beloved and revered by her people, respected by the neighboring tribes... her name had even traveled to faraway lands, earning her a bit of renown and fame.

She still visited the shadow every year, bringing with her stories of her people. One time, not long after the Basilisk had been slain, she came to his cave in a mood that seemed both joyful and melancholic.

"My firstborn is getting married, Shadow."

She smiled joyfully, tears glistening in her eyes.

"He is going to leave the tribe. His bride is from the Otter tribe... they live so far away. When will I see him again?"

Tatal lowered her head.

“I am so happy for him, but I am also so sad. Ah, Shadow... when did life become so complicated?"

Another year, when Tatal came to visit him, her expression was thoughtful.

"Do you know, Shadow? Guests came to the tribe this year. They are people who travel the land, doing nothing but exchanging things. They bartered numerous wondrous items, and they were also interested in purchasing a great deal of things from us... I never really thought about it, but many things we have or make here would seem wondrous to someone else."

She chuckled.

“But they also brought stories. There was a war between the Wolf Tribe and the Elk Tribe, it seems. Seven tribes have come together to build a great temple, somewhere far away, in the lands our ancestors left. The Goddess of the Moon has given birth to a human child. One of the First Humans, a man named Kanakht, is said to have defied the will of the heavens. The world is so vast, Shadow... it makes me so curious. It makes me feel happy to be alive."

Another year, Tatal came bearing gifts.

"Look, Shadow!"

The shadow looked, feeling perplexed.

"What is it?"

Tatal raised the item higher.

“It's called a pillow! There are goose feathers inside. My youngest daughter made it — you are supposed to put your head on it when you sleep. She also did the embroidery!"

Nothing she said made the shadow feel less bewildered.

“I know what a pillow is. Why are you waving it around?"

Tatal blinked a couple of times.

“Well, I just thought... there's nothing but cold stones in your cave. So, I brought you a pillow, for you to rest more comfortably..."

The shadow had to refuse her gift.

He did, however, express his gratitude. Even if he did not have a head to rest on a pillow, the gesture itself, no matter how misguided, was quite sweet.

...He did get the impression that Tatal just wanted to brag about her youngest daughter, though.

Tatal's children grew up. After the firstborn, others had their weddings as well. Her husband retired from being the chieftain and dedicated himself to teaching the young members of the tribe. A new chieftain was selected to replace him, this one coming from a different family.

There were troubles and losses, too. Mystical beasts sometimes set their sights on the tribe's people. Creatures of Corruption — those weak enough for the shadow to ignore — prowled in the darkness. The more Tatal's tribe possessed, the more members of other tribes looked at it with envy.

She had to mediate conflicts at times. At times, she had to take up her bow and her spear, venturing into the forest to fight dangerous creatures. But no matter what happened, Tatal always managed to emerge victorious.

Her fame and reputation slowly grew.

Her power grew, as well.

This primal world was harsh and full of peril, so those who challenged it had no choice but to be tempered by its trials. And so, one day, before the shadow could even consider it, Tatal's soul tore through the boundary of her mortal body, and she became Transcendent — the first Transcendent of her tribe, as well as of all the other tribes in this remote land.

Her Transcendent form was that of a great, magnificent fox.

When Tatal became a Transcendent, there was a great celebration among her people. Beings like her were not unheard of among humans — there had been a lot of them among the mythical First Humans, and there were some among the older tribes that populated distant realms. But in this land, she was the first.

The people who lived here had only ever heard about Transcendent humans in myths and legends. So, they were full of exhilaration and awe.

The shadow, naturally, had an entirely different perspective.

But, still...

He was happy, too.

Because Transcendent beings lived longer lives. That meant that Tatal would be by his side for a bit longer, too.

The tribe was almost unrecognizable by then. What had started as a small scattering of crude tents was now a thriving village with homes built from wood and clay. The tiny pieces of land the tribesmen farmed had turned into vast fields. There were pens for cattle, chickens, and geese.

The crude flint weapons the hunters had used were replaced with copper blades. Instead of hide and fur, they now wore garments made of fabric — some woven out of plants, some out of wool.

Even the wolf-dogs who had been companions of humans for the longest time seemed different, somehow.

The shadow sighed.

‘In the blink of an eye...’

All of this had happened in the blink of an eye.

He was almost worried to imagine what would happen if he closed his eyes and took a little nap.

--- Chapter 3177 ---

Time passed.

The world changed, but the shadow stayed the same.

Hidden in the depths of a dark cave, he rested and experienced the changes through his senses. The trees he remembered as young saplings had become towering giants, then withered and died; new beasts were born as others grew frail and were devoured.

People changed most of all.

Out there in the vast and terrifying expanse of the world, countless humans struggled to establish a foothold against the terrifying Creatures of Corruption across numerous realms. Their tribes were wiped out one after another, only for new ones to arrive in search of a home. Humanity had no advantage in this bloody war — in fact, it was hopelessly outmatched.

But humans persisted. They hid, they learned, they endured... but most of all, they changed.

Humans were a supremely adaptable species, after all. That was what made them so deadly.

In the lands where there was snow and vicious cold, humans learned how to stay warm. In the realms covered by water, they learned how to build rafts and canoes. Their flint weapons were replaced by copper blades; their gatherers had become farmers, while their hunters had become beast tamers.

Crafts, farming, animal husbandry... they were learning it all, desperately trying to survive in a world that had no place for them. In hostile, unknown and unfathomable lands, humans were surrounded by darkness on all sides. They had to sustain themselves and push the darkness back, lest it swallow them.

But the darkness always came back to avenge itself.

The people of Tatal's tribe had an easier time than most because of the shadow. While they still had to fight the Creatures of Corruption, no abomination powerful enough to destroy the tribe without giving it a fighting chance ever appeared in their lands. They were protected by a Shaper of considerable strength, as well — great shaman Tatal, who had slain the Basilisk and became Transcendent.

Because of that, the influence of the Shadow Tribe grew, and soon, the neighboring tribes came to rely on it. Even people from the faraway lands that lay beyond the shadow's senses sometimes came to pay Tatal respect and ask for her advice or assistance.

She gave both freely.

For a long while, life was good. Tatal enjoyed the golden years of her life surrounded by people who admired and loved her. Her tribe thrived, while her family grew.

Her children married one after another. The boys went to live with other tribes, while the girls welcomed their husbands home. Soon enough, Tatal became a grandmother — and before too long, there were a dozen or more of her grandchildren running around a handful of tribes.

Despite being such a prolific grandma, Tatal still looked quite young — she was a Transcendent, after all. If one did not know better, they would have thought that she and her daughters were sisters, while her husband was their father.

The young Wolf, now known as Stone Hand, was not so young anymore. His mighty figure was still straight and imposing, but his hair and beard had long turned grey. After losing an arm to the stone curse of the Basilisk, he had surrendered his position of chieftain and became a teacher for the youths of the tribe. Many of the adult members of the tribe had been his students once, so there were few elders more respected than him.

Despite how different they looked now, Tatal and her husband still lived in perfect harmony. It was just that many things were slowly becoming difficult for him, so she had to assist her aging husband in mundane tasks from time to time — other times, their grandchildren would assist him in her place.

Their home was always full of the sound of children laughing.

When Tatal visited the shadow, there was always a bright smile on her face.

“I am so happy, Shadow. I couldn't be any happier, I think. Life is so harsh, but it is also so impossibly wonderful..."

The shadow was content, as well. He was enjoying this measured, peaceful existence. However, time continued to pass, and things continued to change.

Nothing ever stayed the same.

Soon enough, Tatal's husband passed away from old age, surrounded by his children and grandchildren. The whole tribe mourned his death, and he was buried with the highest honors they knew how to give. Both as his wife and the shaman, Tatal performed the rituals to send his shadow off to the Realm of Death.

Standing above the grave in the ornate garment of the shaman, Tatal looked like a young woman as she buried her old husband. Her radiance was striking, and there was not a single grey hair on her head... she looked far younger than her daughters, even, as if time had no power over her.

The shadow thought that she handled the loss of her husband quite well. She still smiled warmly every time she visited, full of joy and hunger for life...

But he also noticed that her smile was never the same since that day.

There was always a tiny hint of melancholy hidden behind its radiant splendor, as if she couldn't help but feel a little sad even in her happiest moments.

In time, Tatal's village grew into a small town. The wooden and clay huts were replaced by homes built of stone. There was a watermill standing above a stream nearby, and a tall palisade with watchful sentries. Tatal's grandchildren had their own children now. Many of them married into distant tribes, so her bloodline spread far and wide, giving birth to exceptional individuals in many places. Some had even found their way to distant realms, carrying her legacy with them.

But Transcendents lived long lives. Having buried her husband, Tatal eventually buried her children as well. She had managed to maintain her composure when the old Wolf passed away... but even her stalwart heart bled when she heard the news of her firstborn son leaving for the Realm of Shadows, somewhere far away. When she lowered her daughters into the ground one after another, caressing their thin and grey hair.

One time, she cried in the shadow's embrace once again, her bitter wails echoing between the walls of the dark cave. The next time, she faced him with a faltering smile...

On that day, the shadow noticed that there were grey streaks in her own hair now, as well.

He comforted her as best he could. He did not know much about human emotions, but it seemed that his company — his mere existence — was of great comfort to Tatal, in and of itself.

But the shadow himself was uncomfortable. He was restless and worried, unable to find peace.

Time continued its merciless march. Many years passed, and in what felt like an instant, as the shadow watched, Tatal grew old. Her fiery hair had turned grey, and the lines on her face grew deeper.

One time, as she came to visit him, Tatal sat down, supporting her knees, and let out a sigh.

“Ha... climbing this mountain is not as easy as it used to be, Shadow."

Then, she flashed him a smile — the same unabashed, mischievous smile the little girl who had snuck into his cave once showed him. At that moment, the marks of old age covering her face seemed to disappear, and she looked just like that small, frustrating child once more. The two were indistinguishable from each other.

Despite her age, Tatal was still a Transcendent. So, no kind of mountain could strain her.

The shadow smiled in the darkness.

“Shall I make the mountain shorter? I can crush it to pieces, if you want."

Tatal laughed.

“No, no... please don't. I love this mountain. So many things have changed, but the mountain is still the same. We are old friends, she and I."

Tatal remained silent for a few moments, then smiled.

"The world is so different now, Shadow. Sometimes, I remember how it was when I was a little girl... it's almost unrecognizable. The forest where I used to search for berries is gone. The tent where my mother nurtured me only exists in my memory. Our tribe is so large now... and it's populated by strange people. They admire me, they love me... and I love them too. But — and please don't tell anyone — I have to put in some effort to remember all their names and faces."

Her voice was wistful.

The shadow scoffed.

“Whom would I tell? I only ever talk to you."

Tatal grinned.

“That's true."

Her smile seemed to dim a little then, and she looked away.

After remaining silent for a while, Tatal sighed.

“Everyone I knew is gone, Shadow. None of them had the decency to stay alive a little longer."

Then, she looked at the darkness and smiled.

“Only you remain. Am I not lucky, to have such a loyal friend?"

The shadow was not sure how to answer. Eventually, he shrugged mentally.

"I guess. As far as friends go, I am quite a catch."

He paused for a moment, hesitating, and then added in a voice that was quieter than his usual cold tone:

“And you, as well. I must have great luck myself to have a friend such as you."

Tatal laughed once again.

“Naturally! You must be the luckiest shadow in the world!"

Gradually, her laughter quieted down, and she continued to look into the darkness with a smile.

But then, a hint of wistfulness found its way into her shining eyes.

Tatal sighed and looked away, brushing her grey hair back.

She remained silent for a long while, and then said quietly, her voice full of a strange longing.

"I wish... I never became Transcendent, Shadow. Not always, but sometimes, I do."

It was then that the shadow realized that their time together was running short. Tatal did not succumb to age swiftly. But to the shadow, it seemed like everything happened in the blink of an eye. Before he even knew what to say, what to do, her back became bent, and the lines on her face turned into deep wrinkles. Her grey hair turned frail and white, and her startling radiance gave place to the look of a wizened elder.

The great shaman, Tatal, was old now. She was ancient. Having become a living legend to the people of her tribe — and all the tribes in the surrounding lands — she was treated with utmost reverence by all people. Her descendants were everywhere. Some of them were pillars of the Shadow Tribe, some had scattered across faraway lands and distant realms.

Some of them had even forged legends of their own.

During the day, she was surrounded by boisterous children and people who loved her. Everywhere she went, she was met with respect and admiration. Tatal seemed to have grown comfortable with old age, having nothing but warm smiles to share with people. It looked like she had fathomed some kind of arcane wisdom that the shadow couldn't quite discern.

Otherwise, how could she remain so content and peaceful?

The closer the end of her life drew, the less peaceful the shadow became. In fact, he had forgotten the meaning of peace, spending his days in turmoil.

‘Not yet. Not yet... it must not happen yet...’

But then, a day came when Old Tatal couldn't rise from her bed anymore. It was a great shock to the people of the tribe, and they gathered around her family home in a crowd, silently praying for her recovery. Those of her descendants who lived nearby rushed back to the lands of the Shadow Tribe, many of them harboring precious memories of being cared for by their kind, wise ancestor as a child.

Tatal was never alone, her dying bed surrounded by a crowd of friends and loved ones.

But it seemed that the spark of Flame that was the source of her life had waned too much. Now, it shimmered weakly, faltering, ready to be extinguished.

As the night fell, the shadow left his cave for the second time since the dawn of existence and made his way to the room where Tatal lay in the darkness, her small figure hidden by the blankets on the bed she had shared once with the young Wolf. Her eyes had grown weak with age, and yet, she still felt his presence.

Tatal smiled.

“Shadow... you came."

He manifested himself into a vaguely human shape at her bedside.

Looking down, the shadow spoke:

“Of course."

The old woman lying on the bed laughed quietly.

“All these years, all the times I visited your home... and this is the first time you came to mine. I'm happy."

Her breathing was weak and strained, but her smile was relaxed and joyful.

“I am so happy to see you, my friend. One last time."

The shadow looked around.

Tatal's descendants and disciples slept restlessly outside. Beyond the walls of her family home, the members of the tribe were holding a vigil. It seemed like all the people in the land had gathered to see her go... But he wasn't ready.

“It doesn't have to be the last time."

His voice, which had always been cold, suddenly sounded ragged.

The shadow hesitated.

“If you... if you want to... I can take your shadow into my soul. You can stay there forever. At peace, unchanging. With me."

Tatal studied him for a long time, her smile gentle.

Then, with a sigh, she looked away and shook her head.

"To exist forever? Never changing, never knowing anything but peace? That... sounds so terribly sad, Shadow. I don't want it. I wouldn't wish it on my enemy."

She paused for a moment, catching her breath, and chuckled.

“Thank you. But I am content with where I am... where I have been. I am already at peace. I'm happy."

Tatal turned to look at him, and even though there was contentment in her eyes... there was also a hint of regret. After staying silent for a while, she said quietly:

“I only worry about you, Shadow."

The shadow was bewildered.

Ever since she was a little girl, Tatal had always had a talent for leaving him confused and speechless.

Finally, he found the strength to speak:

“Me? You are about to die, and you worry about me?"

Tatal nodded.

“Of course. I worry... that you'll be all alone without me, Shadow.”

The shadow stared at her, expressionless. He had not even known the concept of loneliness before Tatal came to his cave. So, he had never been lonely.

...But he knew that he would be, once she was gone.

Met with his silence, Tatal sighed.

Her eyes were growing unfocused.

In a weak, faltering tone, she whispered.

“Take care of yourself, my friend. And thank you. Thank you for being my companion on this long, thorny path. For... being my friend. I would have been all alone without you, too."

Tatal's eyes closed slowly.

“It was a... long and wondrous... life. Wasn't it? But... I'm tired now. I'm ready."

The shadow knelt and held her hand.

He held it until dawn broke.

By then, Tatal's breath was gone, and her shadow had left, leaving him all alone in the darkness.

The shadow let go then and rose, looking around the unfamiliar room. He noticed something on a shelf by her bedside. An old, ancient... incredibly ugly doll.

He took it, his hand trembling.

A few moments later, the shadow was back in his cave.

The mountain shook slightly, and the sky was suddenly obscured by stormy clouds, a terrible rain descending on the earth from the heavens.

Hidden in the darkness, the shadow placed the doll near a silver bell that lay on a protruding stone.

Then, he dismissed his human form, hiding himself deeper.

‘Never, never...'

He never wanted to befriend a human again.

Humans were such fragile things. They appeared and vanished in the blink of an eye.

But his memories of them, his love for them, remained forever.

At that moment, he realized something.

It was that, perhaps, the affection of mortals was just as dangerous to the gods as divine benevolence was to mortals.

But he did not care.

All he knew was that there was no Tatal in this world anymore.

And without her, the world was colder.

--- Chapter 3178 ---

The shadow retreated into his cave. He hid himself in the darkness.

Without Tatal, the world did not interest him anymore. And since Tatal did not come to visit him, the world did not invade his home, either.

He sensed the lands around him undergoing changes, but all of it left him indifferent.

In the darkness, the shadow glanced at the ugly doll. Then, he picked up the silver bell and shook it faintly.

He remembered...

In one of his lives, he lived in a gorgeous city that sprawled across dozens of flying islands, built of ivory stone. The city was prosperous, and his life was one of abundance. However, he was mad... everyone in the city was, and in the surrounding lands, as well.

His wife was mad, too. Theirs was a happy madness.

If there was one sorrow that darkened their blissful insanity, it was that the gods had not granted them children. They prayed, they waited, but it was all for naught... until, one day, a miracle happened.

After long years of bitter failures, his wife became pregnant.

The day his daughter was born, he was so happy that his heart was ready to jump out of his chest. His daughter was a miraculous child... a blessed child. And as she grew up, she only became more lovely.

Such a lovely child could have one fate — the most wonderful one of them all.

To be sacrificed to the Ivory Lord, the dragon.

Such honor!

On the day his daughter was chained to the blackened stone in front of the great tower, he smiled brightly. His wife was full of mirth, as well.

And when the dragon's flame swallowed their child...

Ah!

He was the happiest he had ever been. He was beyond himself, so much so that his smile had become painful.

...The shadow stirred, disgusted.

Yes, that was what he felt — disgust. He had never felt it before, but its bitter taste was familiar.

He did not want to remember such filthy, vile lives.

But the torrent of memories was merciless. In another life, the shadow was a proud and powerful warrior, a maiden from an ancient sect who venerated War God. But she was mad, as well.

All of them were.

The people from the surrounding lands brought orphaned girls to their temple, to be raised by the War Maidens and become devoted priestesses of War — especially those born with red hair.

She loved the children.

The other priestesses were harsh, and some of them were indifferent. But she cared for these girls, because she had been one of them herself — a long time ago. And so, she spent more time with them than the rest.

She was also far more motivated to make them worthy of the gorgeous, glorious legacy of their ancient sect. To make them strong enough to be beloved by War. Sadly... the children were weak and fragile. They were lazy. They failed to understand the honor of their station, and some were oblivious to their duty.

So, she taught them. Some survived her teaching, and some didn't. She mourned the latter, and redoubled her efforts to guide the former. She wanted them to succeed. She was full of desire to make them stronger. Stronger than the wicked traitor in the west, at least — strong enough to please their goddess. Desire, desire...

Desire burned her heart and blackened her gaze, turning her into something twisted. But, by then, her mind was already too far gone.

And, in the end, so were the children.

The shadow threw the silver bell away.

He had learned what disgust meant.

But now, he also knew what wrath was.

Full of disgust and anger, the shadow curled into a mass of darkness and trembled.

Cold, cold...

His cave was so cold now. It had never been that way before.

‘I want to rest.'

The shadow closed its mind and forced itself into a state of half-slumber.

And yet, even in that passive state, it could still feel the world changing.

Time was flowing swiftly on the outside. Now that Tatal was gone, the Shadow Tribe had chosen a new shaman... then another, then another. They came and went, indistinguishable from each other. They bowed in front of his cave and left offerings. No one dared to enter his cave anymore. No one dared to steal the offerings and eat them while giggling and swaying their little feet, either.

The shadow ignored it all.

Out there in the valley, the town grew. The people of the tribe learned new crafts and developed what they had already mastered. Bronze came to replace copper; mines and quarries were established in the mountains. Swift boats traveled up and down the rivers, carrying goods to and from distant tribes. The garments that the tribesmen wore changed, becoming more refined and tasteful. The interiors of their homes were decorated with items that considered beauty, not just utility. There were more Awakened among them now, as well as more Ascended. Eventually, there was even a Transcendent or two.

Soon enough, the town became a city.

By then, the Shadow Tribe was not really a tribe anymore — it was a small, young nation. Having absorbed the surrounding tribes and expanded its lands, they were swiftly approaching the point of becoming a city-state.

The shadow felt that the Age of Gods was swiftly approaching its end, ready to give way to the Age of Heroes — the age when humanity had already established a foothold in the world, and its Transcendent champions battled the Creatures of Corruption for dominion over it.

Somewhere far away, Kanakht must have already created the first human kingdom... But, strangely enough, the shadow never heard the name of Kanakht being mentioned. The former tribesmen were in contact with many other people, receiving news from countless mortal realms. And yet, there was no news of the first human Supreme expanding his Domain.

Instead of him, they only talked about a beautiful, dreadful creature called the White Abyss — a thing that was not human, and yet seemed to have established the first human kingdom... or have usurped it, at least.

The shadow was mildly surprised, since that differed from the fragmented memories of the future contained in his mind. But then again, some of the futures he remembered contradicted each other, so he simply accepted it as one of such discrepancies. He did not care, either way.

He did not even care about the flourishing city that grew near his cave.

Out there in the city, Tatal's descendants — the branches of her family that stayed in the tribe — were still prospering. However, he did not feel anything for them. These people were all strangers to him, after all. The shadow had felt some connection to her children, but they were long gone.

Now, those who called themselves the heirs of the Great Shaman did not even know what she had looked like.

If anything, the shadow disliked them.

As the fortune of the tribe improved and its life became more prosperous, its people slowly changed. The many temptations of civilization — wealth, power, vice — took root in their hearts. The descendants of Tatal wielded far more power than most... And power corrupted.

So, slowly, they became prideful and conceited, believing that they were better than the common folk.

The shadow did not care about the failings of humans, and yet he could not help but feel dismayed by these ones in particular, since they were dirtying the memory of his dear friend with their every action.

Tatal had been kind, but these people were cruel. Tatal had been selfless and generous, but these people were full of selfish avarice. Tatal had treated every person as an equal despite her great strength, but these ones glanced down at others despite being pathetic and weak.

The other people of the city were not much different.

The more the shadow looked, the more disgusted he became.

And so, not wishing to feel that way anymore, he turned his gaze away from the world.

He withdrew his senses, confining them to the darkness of his cave.

He thought that he would find peace then. But instead, he only felt lonely.

The shadow rested in the darkness, blind to the world.

He refused the call of his past lives, unwilling to remember them.

Instead, he remembered Tatal.

In his mind, he could still hear her bright voice. He could still see her and smell her scent. He could still feel her warmth.

That was a happy place.

So, for a while, the shadow indulged in dreams about the past.

A long time passed that way...

Until, one day, the shadow was disturbed by a familiar scent.

There was the scent of blood drifting into his cave. The scent of death...

Frowning, the shadow stirred, slowly shaking off his slumber, and directed his senses outward.

What he saw there made the unfathomable darkness of his being boil.

Out there, on the altar in front of his cave... There was a human body lying motionlessly, blood flowing onto the cold stone.

There were empty eyes staring at the indifferent sky.

There were other humans, as well — dressed in magnificent clothes, standing around the altar. One of them held a bloodied knife; the rest were bowing toward the cave, reciting prayers.

Some had prideful, arrogant smiles hiding behind the solemn expressions plastered across their faces.

"For you, oh Dark One! Like the Great Shaman before us, we plead for your favor!"

The shadow lost the ability to think for a moment.

Images flashed in his mind...

The flames of the ivory dragon.

The orphaned girls smiling tentatively on the doorstep of an old temple.

He remembered Tatal.

Kind Tatal, who had been tortured by the necessary death of a single murderer. Who refused to ask him for help in the battle against the Basilisk, knowing the price of taking a life.

The shadow remembered a gaunt man digging graves in the frozen soil on the shore of an ice-covered ocean.

And then, the shadow remembered wrath. He remembered madness.

'How DARE THEY!'

He moved.

The mountain shook when the shadow left his cave. Only, this time, he did not take the form of a human.

Instead, the shadow revealed himself in front of these people in his true form — as an endless, unfathomable, titanic torrent of darkness.

As death.

He had made Tatal a promise once, didn't he? He had sent her people a message. And he was a very honest shadow, indeed.

How short their memory was...

The shadow washed over the world.

‘Die.'

And as he willed it, everything died.

The people in front of the altar collapsed like marionettes whose strings had been cut.

The people in the city below fell, too.

The cattle in the pens, the dogs guarding the homes, the mice hidden in the walls, the ants scurrying to steal crumbs from the floor.

The wheat in the fields withered and turned into dust. The trees, the grass, the flowers — all of it died, leaving nothing but desolate emptiness in its wake.

‘Why can't they just leave me alone?’

The shadow drowned the dead city, as well as the lands that surrounded it.

He was tired of life... of the living.

He just wanted peace, so why was it so hard for these revolting things to stop bothering him?

Soon enough, the land was entirely dead, enveloped in impenetrable darkness.

The city was perfectly preserved, but it was entirely empty as well, swallowed by shadows.

It was silent.

And then, there was finally peace.

--- Chapter 3179 ---

The land was shrouded in darkness.

The world was still and silent, devoid of life. The shadow beheld the silent world and felt at peace.

'Yes... this is good. I like it better.'

There were no humans to disturb him with their noise, with their greed, with their worship... with their blazing, desperate desires. There were no trees, no grass, no beasts, no vermin. There was no chaos — there were only shadows.

The shadow had wanted to become one with the world, dissolving in its endless changes. But now, he was the world. It was a different kind of unity, but one that he found himself more fond of.

Everything was as it should be, since there was nothing to impose on his tranquility. And yet...

Somewhere deep, deep within the shadow's vast and ancient being, he felt a hint of a strange emotion.

Was it regret? Or guilt? Or perhaps horror?

The shadow did not know what guilt and regret were, so he wasn't sure.

He did not care to find out, either.

He simply wanted to enjoy his peace. Eventually, the land transformed.

The shadows surged, and countless shapes rose from them. Black trees swayed in the wind, their black leaves rustling to create a soothing melody. Black flowers bloomed beautifully in the darkness. The city was now populated by myriad shades — the shades went about their business, mimicking the mundane actions of the living.

It was just that they were silent.

The shadow was in absolute control of this dark and eerie realm. So, he could observe it without feeling disturbed, time flowing past his small island of tranquility.

‘Why did I kill them?'

At some point, he asked himself that question.

The shadow did not feel uncomfortable with his decision. The disappearance of the nascent nation had only brought him peace and relief. He had experienced countless lives, after all... he had existed for myriad years. To him, the lives of humans were brief and fleeting — a dozen generations would be born and die in a flash, devoid of meaning.

All humans died, and most of them died swiftly. He merely hastened their deaths by an instant, replacing the turmoil of their lives with eternal peace.

Just like a human would not feel much after stepping on an anthill, the shadow was not someone who concerned himself with the fate of humans.

At least he had not been, once.

The being who he had been once would not have destroyed the city, though. At most, he would have wiped out the priests and supplicants who had sacrificed a life to him — simply to avoid further annoyance.

But, at some point, something about him changed.

What was it?

After considering it for a long while, the shadow came to the conclusion that it was all because of his friend, Tatal. Tatal, who had left the mark of humanity on him. Before meeting her, the shadow did not know what loneliness was. He did not know what affection was, either... love, joy, trust, hope. He had become capable of all these emotions because of her.

But those were not the only emotions he had learned.

There was also sorrow, anger, resentment... there was hatred.

It was hatred that he had felt on that dark day.

So, in an ironic twist of fate, the shadow had not destroyed these people because he was like a deity. He had destroyed them because he had been overcome by anger...

Which was the most human thing he had ever done.

Coming to that conclusion left the shadow in low spirits. Observing his lifeless kingdom, he asked himself an old question once again.

‘What am I?'

The shadow was not quite mortal. But he wasn't a deity, either... just a forlorn being stuck somewhere in between.

Left alone in his silent kingdom, ruling it like a god, the shadow found a measure of peace.

But peace did not feel as joyous anymore. And so, for whatever reason, the shadow remembered one of his past lives.

In that life, he had been born as a prince. The nation his father ruled was small, but prosperous... it had been once, at least. By the time he was born, the kingdom was in decline, and its people were suffering.

That was because the days of its glory were long past. Once, a long time ago, valiant Transcendent heroes defeated the Creatures of Corruption that had ruled the land, allowing its people to flourish. Those heroes were dead, though, or had gone away to seek glory in distant realms. Now, only their descendants remained.

And their descendants, while not as powerful, were many times more power-hungry. Perhaps it was precisely their weakness that made them so insecure, while growing up in the shadow of their great ancestors made them greedy and ambitious.

The nobles lived in luxury, exploiting and tormenting common people. The royal family was the worst of all, while the king — his father — was a vicious, cruel tyrant.

But he... he wanted to be a hero.

He wanted to be someone who helped people, like the great heroes of the past. And yet, there was little he could do. There were different kinds of princes, after all, and he was the weakest among them. His mother wasn't a queen, and neither was she one of the favored concubines — instead, she was a lowly maid who had happened to catch the tyrant's eye.

His childhood was neither lavish nor happy. The other princes all despised and hated each other, endlessly competing for their father's favor. Even if they did not see him as a threat, they could not pass up the chance to elevate themselves by mocking and tormenting him. There was no powerful clan backing him, either, and he was frail. So, he failed every time he tried to stand up for himself.

But he still resisted.

In fact, the more they tried to crush him, the more fiercely he fought for the right to hold his head high.

In the privacy of solitude, though, he could not help but shed bitter tears.

‘Why, why? Why does Father do nothing to stop them? Am I not his son?’

If there was one gift the gods had given him, it was a sharp mind... or maybe he had simply not been given any other choice but to hone his mind, since he had no strength whatsoever to protect himself.

And so, he quickly understood that the vicious princes had become that way very much by his father's design.

A tyrant feared many things, after all... but his powerful, cruel father feared his sons the most.

His father needed the support of the noble clans, so he took their daughters as wives and concubines. However, as soon as an heir was born, he became deathly afraid that the nobles would assassinate him and put the prince of their bloodline on the throne instead.

So, he pitted the princes against each other and cultivated their viciousness, suppressing the noble clans through internal conflict. If the princes could kill each other before growing too powerful, that would be even better — then, he would be able to repeat the cycle with his grandchildren, postponing the time his bloody reign inevitably ended in a coup.

The forlorn prince, the only one of those without backing who survived, smiled bitterly.

Well, then...

Didn't that make him a perfect tool?

He was the only one of the princes whom his father could use without fearing the power of the noble clans. He could become a weapon for the king to use in order to keep the other heirs in check.

All he needed to do was help his father understand his usefulness — without appearing too capable, of course, which would only make the king feel wary of him.

But why would he?

After all, unlike his brothers, he did not want power. He did not want to become king. He just wanted to survive... he wanted to live with a measure of dignity that he believed all people deserved.

That only lasted until he happened to journey outside the castle and saw how the people of the kingdom lived, though. Their desperate plight, their suffering, the inhuman cruelties they were subjected to by the nobles and the king's men...

All of it reminded him of his mother's short and tragic life.

It left him rattled... it made him angry — angrier than he thought he could ever be.

And so, he set a new goal for himself. He decided that it wasn't just him who deserved to survive and live with dignity — it was all people of the kingdom. His people. He decided that he would set them free. And so, using his sharp mind and lack of strength, he slowly earned the attention of his father.

He became the Crown Prince, tasked with suppressing the other heirs.

But, of course, that was only the beginning...

Because all the while, he worked tirelessly to achieve his goal. He cultivated his mind, searched for reliable allies, and won the loyalty of those who wanted to save the kingdom just like he did.

A long time ago, valiant heroes had saved the people from the Creatures of Corruption. Now, he looked for heroes who would save the people from the tyranny of men.

He tried to make himself into a hero, as well. He wanted to bring everyone salvation.

...There was no doubt in his mind that he would succeed.

--- Chapter 3180 ---

If there was one thing he knew, it was that great things couldn't be achieved alone. Even the great gods had banded together to fight the Void — so how could mere mortals like him hope to carry the burden of change on their own?

So, being used as a tool by his father and despised by his brothers, he endured their scorn and set out to find reliable allies in secret.

At first, he found those few among the officials who had not relinquished their honor yet. With their help, he established a small, hidden network of agents and informants. And when information from all corners of the kingdom flowed into his modest courtyard, he identified those who could help him rally the people and stop the tyrant, his father.

The people were not blind to injustice, after all, and strength was not granted exclusively to nobles. There were those among common folk who wielded great power and felt the same way he did — who wanted to help their kingdom, but were granted no recourse.

He approached them in secret, but with a sincere heart. And, perhaps moved by his sincerity, they agreed to join him.

There was a warrior who hunted the Creatures of Corruption in the mountains to protect people.

There was a beautiful and kind priestess of Heart God who soothed those who were in pain.

There was a wise scholar who lived in exile, having been dismissed from court...

And many more.

He gathered them, he won the support of the people, he did his best to protect the kingdom from the atrocities committed by the corrupt nobles.

And, when the moment was right, he rose in rebellion against the king.

The revolt was swift, but bloody — it couldn't have been peaceful, no matter how much he wished that it was. Many of his comrades and companions lost their lives, and at times, it seemed like all of them would perish. But he never lost faith in their cause. He never lost his composure, either, leading the rebels with a clear mind and a steady hand.

In the end, their despair turned to triumph. They won — not only because their cause was virtuous, but also because their adversary was corrupt. In the end, the king could only rely on the princes to suppress the rebellion, but the princes were loyal to no one but themselves. They turned on each other in secret, and in the end, even the king could not save himself from the treachery of his sons.

The weakest of them — the Crown Prince, whom everyone disregarded — was the only victor in the end. With the tyrant dead and the corrupt nobles purged, his comrades bowed as they begged him to take the throne.

Thus, he became king.

Sitting on the throne and feeling the weight of the crown pressing down on him, he felt a sense of bitter irony. He had never wanted to rule, and he had never wanted to spill blood either. But, in the end, such was his fate...

Perhaps that was the only kind of ruler who could be good — someone who did not want the crown, but was forced to put it on for the sake of others.

The rebellion, the coronation — all of it was merely a means to an end. His true goal was to alleviate the suffering of his people, and so, now was the time for his true work to begin.

Having become king, he ruled to the best of his ability. He ruled wisely and with the well-being of his subjects in mind. His former companions became the pillars of the kingdom, and for a long time, life was good.

There were problems, naturally. There were Creatures of Corruption hiding in the darkness, there were natural calamities. There were neighboring kingdoms who looked at what others possessed with greed. But with a wise ruler and powerful champions, his kingdom weathered all storms.

In time, he married his dearest companion, the blessed priestess of Heart God. The wise scholar was his most trusted advisor. The mighty warrior was his general and the leader of the kingdom's defenders. Everything seemed to be going well...

Until, one day, a worm of doubt found its way into his mind.

It began innocently enough. He used to be confident in his decisions, but at some point, he began questioning if he was doing his best. One wrong choice could doom innumerable people, after all — so, it was only natural for him to want to be as diligent as he could be.

But once he began doubting himself, it wasn't long before he began doubting others as well.

After all... if he was mistaken, if some of his decisions did not benefit the kingdom, then why did everyone remain silent?

Did he not have advisors, loyal subjects, and friends? Weren't they supposed to help him keep the kingdom on course?

He became indecisive, often wearing a troubled expression.

Doubt whispered insidiously into his ear.

‘Why has no one spoken out?’

His old comrade, the learned scholar. His wise and gentle wife. His friend, the fearless warrior... why had they ignored all his mistakes?

Was it simply because they had not noticed them? Was their faith in him too strong?

Or did they not care?

...Or was there another, more sinister reason?

That was how he began to doubt even those who were closest to him. And once he began doubting them, he saw things he had not noticed before.

Wasn't his wife laughing too eagerly when conversing with the mighty warrior? Wasn't the warrior standing too closely, and looking at her too often?

‘No, it couldn't be...’

But what if it was?

Wasn't the scholar suggesting reforms that were a little too bold, a little too vague in their implementation? Things that looked innocent in and of themselves, but painted a perilous picture when put together?

Like offering more independence to the warriors of the kingdom. Sure, it would enhance their ability to act swiftly... but wouldn't it also give their leader more control over the kingdom, while stripping authority from the crown?

‘Surely not. And what if it does? I trust my friend implicitly, so why does it matter how much control he has?’

Implicitly...

But why would he need to have independent authority?

Didn't the mighty warrior trust his friend, the king, implicitly as well?

His doubts grew deeper.

After a while, he grew quiet and withdrawn. He observed those around him, and the more he looked, the more their actions strengthened his doubt.

Until his doubt became suspicion.

He suspected that the queen harbored a secret love for the warrior.

He suspected that the warrior wanted the crown for himself.

He suspected that his advisor was cunningly trying to lead him astray.

The court officials, the maids, the soldiers, the priests...

He couldn't trust any of them.

They all wanted to see him gone.

‘How sad.’

In the throes of his suspicion, the king felt heartbroken and full of bitter regret.

He had spilled the blood of his brothers to save the kingdom from the greed of the corrupt nobility and the mad tyrant — of those whose hearts had been corrupted by power. But now that his comrades had tasted power themselves, they seemed to have succumbed to its temptation as well. So, what was he to do?

Defend the kingdom from that corruption? But how?

And so, he began doing things that he had never thought he would do. It was so alien and distasteful, in fact, that at time, he felt like he wasn't the one acting — as if his body moved on its own, his lips twisted into a smile themselves, and the words he spoke came from someone else.

From someone cunning, patient, and infinitely malevolent when it needed to be. He began by subtly manipulating those around him, like he had manipulated his father once. He instilled them with doubt, then turned them against each other, making them believe that there was intrigue and conspiracy abound.

Slowly, the atmosphere in the court changed. The previous harmony was gone, replaced by tension and hostility. He used that hostility to suppress the initiatives suggested by his old friend, the wise scholar, pulling the strings from behind the curtain to make it seem like it was the officials who rose against them, not him.

''I just don't understand.' the scholar once told him, full of frustration. 'It's like they all lost their minds!''

The king smiled soothingly, offering him a compassionate hand.

He promised to find out who was turning the court against his most loyal advisor. But, in secret, he began preparations to banish the scholar from court.

Then, he turned his gaze to the warrior.

His greatest champion wielded much more martial power than he himself possessed. So, he couldn't deal with the despicable traitor directly... instead, he used underhanded means to start a conflict with a neighboring kingdom. The battle was eventually won, and the adversary was forced to surrender a considerable tribute.

But, in the process, his general was grievously wounded, diminishing his fearsome strength.

Some soldiers had died in the process, as well as some innocent people. But what was there to do? Their lives were a necessary sacrifice for the future of the kingdom.

"This whole story smells," spoke the warrior, recovering from his wounds in the palace. "We never managed to find the bastards who burned the border village. Could it be that someone else was behind the attack?"

The king put an expression of somber concern on his face.

“If so... then it was someone who wanted to pit our two kingdoms against each other and benefit from the strife. We must stay vigilant in case these sinister forces make another move."

While the warrior was recovering, the queen tended to him — she was a priestess of Heart God, after all, as well as his former comrade.

Still... was there really a need for the queen to play the role of a healer personally?

The king watched silently, a dark and vicious darkness taking root in his heart.

The queen was beloved by the people, and their love alone gave her power and influence. So, he took precautions to undermine that influence.

Dealing with her was the easiest of all — after all, despite all her virtues, the queen had a lethal weakness. It was that she had failed to give him a heir. So, he spread a rumor that the queen was barren, pushing a few court officials into demanding that he take a second wife.

He rebuked them publicly, naturally...

But the damage was already done.

The queen's influence was shaken.

''Those vicious snakes!' the queen pleaded, both angered and hurt. 'How... how dare they!''

He held her in a loving embrace.

"Shh, my love. Don't listen to those fools. You are the only one for me — you know you are, forever..."

Just like that, all those who threatened his position were suppressed. If he wanted to get rid of them, all he had to do was twist the mood in the court faintly. He could banish the scholar; he could dismiss the warrior from his post. He could replace the queen with a new wife, sending her to spend the rest of her life in the Heart God's temple.

He was safe... and therefore, the kingdom was safe.

But, despite that, his doubts did not disappear.

They only grew stronger.

After all... why would he send the scholar away? Why would he dismiss the warrior? Why would he let the treacherous queen go?

So that they could unite and conspire against him together, just like they had done in the past?

And what about the court officials, who hid greed and ambition behind masks of loyalty?

What about the maid, the soldiers, the priests?

All of them... all of them...

All of them conspired against him.

All of them were waiting for the moment to bring him down.

The soldiers glanced at him when they thought he could not see, hiding vicious snarls. The court officials whispered in dark corridors, discussing treacherous schemes. The maids watched him like hawks as they served him food, as if choosing which dish to poison. The priests manipulated the minds of the people, hiding their ambitions behind the names of the gods.

His former friends were the worst of them all.

They were all traitors...

They all wanted to see him gone.

So, he did what he needed to do to protect himself.

On a dark winter night, he ordered the gates of the castle to be barred. The soldiers seemed confused by the order, but followed it anyway — he killed them as soon as the gates were lowered, destroying the mechanism that would allow someone to raise them again.

Then, he made his way to his living quarters.

The queen was still awake, so she smiled when he sat on the bed near her and reached forward to hug her.

Her smile faltered when his hands wrapped around her neck.

“M-my... my king!"

He returned the smile as he strangled the traitor, easily overpowering her attempts to break free.

It was peculiar, though... the queen was of a higher Rank than he was, so she should have been able to overpower him. However, a dire strength overcame him, turning his grip into an iron vice. No matter how she struggled, it was all for naught.

It must have been virtue that aided him, while her own strength was stolen by treachery.

“My... m—my king..."

Once the queen was dead, he finally felt some of his doubt subsiding.

‘Ah...’

He should have done this a long time ago. He should have killed them all.

And so, he did.

His friend, the warrior, was still weak from his wounds. So, it wasn't that hard to carve him into pieces with a sharp blade.

The scholar was supposed to be wise, and yet he failed to predict the moment of his death. Once his corpse fell to the floor, his skull split open, the king smiled.

"Traitors, traitors..."

There were traitors everywhere.

And so, he killed them all — the soldiers, the maids, the officials, the priests.

During the darkest hours of the night, the castle was full of screams of terror. Some tried to run, some tried to resist... but they all died, in the end. That was because he was suddenly full of an awful, insurmountable power.

When everyone was dead, he stood in the middle of the throne room, covered in blood.

He was laughing... laughing in relief.

‘Oh, right. There is one more traitor left...’

There was one more person he doubted. So, he raised his blade and brought it down on his own head, splitting it open.

Blood poured from the wound.

Something else poured out of it, as well...

‘What is it?'

It was silk.

Beautiful black silk spilled to the floor, blood glistening on its fine threads like jewels. Then, something moved inside his head, and a breathtaking creature emerged. Spreading its wings and shaking the blood, the bone shards, and the brain matter off them, it leaped off his head and soared into the air.

The king watched the beautiful moth fly, his eyes full of wonder.

‘So beautiful.’

He smiled before falling down.

The last thing he saw before being blinded by the dark splendor of the moth was its graceful silhouette disappearing into the vastness of the starry sky beyond the window.

'No...'

He didn't want to be apart from it.

He wanted to pursue it... to find it again... So, as his dead body began to twist and reshape itself, the king climbed the wall and dove into the window.

He rushed toward the distant mountains.

However, even as thousands of years passed...

He had never caught sight of the beautiful moth again.

--- Chapter 3181 ---

The shadow remembered his life as the righteous king who had been devoured by doubt.

He remembered his life as the worm of doubt that had devoured the king, as well. He remembered being the hideous creature the king had become...

And the radiant, sinister moth that had crawled out of the king's broken skull, too. The two couldn't be more different. But, for the shadow, they were one and the same. He had lived both of their long and terrifying lives, after all, so he knew. He knew that the moth had wanted to live just as desperately as the king had.

All living things were enthralled by life, and all living things were terrified of death. Except for him.

The shadow was weary of life and denied death, so there was no escape from his endless existence. There was only the tranquil peace of his lifeless kingdom and the unwelcome torment of his memories. He remembered being the moth...

The eerie creature had been insidious, but young and weak. After gaining its dark wings in the chrysalis of the king's ravaged mind, it escaped into the vast, cruel world beyond. It wanted to live, so it wanted to become stronger... to grow. And so, it did, moving across countless realms like a calamity.

Until it became a profane deity, the sinister Spirit of Doubt.

If the shadow wanted to, he could have remembered every detail of its ghastly Apotheosis. But he turned his thoughts away from those memories — not only because a terrifying abyss of Corruption was hidden in them, but also because he had no use for such knowledge.

Even if he wanted to become a god, he wouldn't go about it the same ghastly way the moth had.

‘Still, I wonder...’

There was another memory he was wary of. An event his very being resisted remembering.

It was the day the Spirit of Doubt met the Demon of Fate.

Sprawled across his lifeless realm, encompassing it, the shadow shivered.

‘Weaver...’

Even if he did not know why, he feared the nebulous daemon more than he feared the gods and all other deities.

Perhaps it was because something moved within his soul every time he thought about Weaver, as if it was pierced by an infinite number of golden strings.

The gods were dreadful, but fate was more frightening than the gods.

The Spirit of Doubt had suffered after making a deal with Weaver.

‘Have I met Weaver once, as well?'

That would explain his pitiful fate. Unnerved, the shadow cleansed his mind of all thoughts. It was dangerous to think about gods too loudly, after all... what if they heard him?

Instead, the shadow thought back to the life of the unfortunate king.

The shadow felt like he had been plagued by doubt too, a long time ago.

But eventually, he seemed to have learned trust.

Trust was a weapon that allowed him to prevail over doubt and saved him from eventually sharing a fate similar to that of the king. It allowed him to... do what?

To be cast by another, perhaps.

The shadow did not remember.

With a sigh, he turned his attention to the simple, entertaining existence of shades populating his kingdom.

Time passed.

The shadow's existence was peaceful and empty. Nothing disturbed him — apart from weary wanderers who sometimes came to his dark land, then fled in terror.

Well, and something else.

At some point, a worm of doubt found its way into the shadow's mind.

It wasn't a sinister Creature of Corruption, but rather a mundane suspicion.

The shadow wasn't sure that he was right, or how it could even be possible...

But he began to suspect there was something still clinging to life, somehow, in the dead darkness of his peaceful kingdom.

***

Far away, in a distant realm, a magnificent city sprawled under the vast sky. At the heart of the city stood a towering pyramid, its surface clad in great plates of smooth, polished stone. The pinnacle of the pyramid was encased in sheets of purest gold, and in the brilliant light of the sun, it shone with a blinding white radiance.

It was as if the pyramid was wreathed in flame; as if there was another sun burning at its tip, reflecting the glory of its celestial sister.

That was the temple and palace of the White Abyss, from which she ruled the First Kingdom.

At the moment, an elderly priest was climbing the steps of the pyramid.

He was sweating profusely, enduring the unbearable heat. His eyes were covered by a blindfold — without it, he would have been blinded by the pristine radiance of his goddess. The pyramid was tall, and the priest was old... if not for his Rank, he would have perished on the endless steps, as countless supplicants had perished before him.

But, in the end, the old priest made it to the wide platform at the end of the great stairs. Letting out a relieved sigh, he knelt in front of the golden palace hidden inside the upper part of the pyramid.

The towering gates of the palace were open, and if one was bold enough, they could try to steal a glimpse of what lay inside. However, they wouldn't see anything — because there was nothing inside the palace except an ocean of immolating white flame.

That ocean of living flame was the true form of the White Abyss — the beautiful, dreadful queen of the First Kingdom.

The priest remained on his knees for a long while, catching his breath. Then, he pressed his forehead against the scorching stones.

"My lady, One Who Brings Light, the Eternal Flame, the Tyrant of Compassion, oh great White Abyss... I beseech thee..."

There was silence for a long time, disturbed

only by the roaring rustle of the dancing flames.

Then, the low roar of the flames coalesced into a clear, inhuman voice.

“What is your desire?"

The priest trembled, overcome by awe. He remained motionless for a few moments, composing himself, then spoke in a reverent tone:

“My lady, there is news from the distant reaches of your kingdom. The realm boundary is weakened, and the influence of the Void is spreading across the border regions. We are afraid that a powerful Creature of Corruption has set its sights on your people and is soon to arrive. Please, my lady! Descend from your throne and bestow your blessing upon the unworthy! Show us the brilliance of your purifying wrath!"

There was silence once more.

Then, the priest felt the unbearable heat abating, somewhat, and the roaring of flame growing quieter.

He heard the sound of light footsteps approaching him from the gates of the palace.

As they did, he felt his soul igniting with unbearable longing. Piety, greed, devotion, ambition, love, lust — all of his wants blazed with fiery intensity, making him grit his teeth and press himself lower harder on the stone.

"Remove your blindfold.”

The priest hesitated, then followed the command spoken in a clear, beautiful voice with a trembling hand. He still did not dare to raise his gaze, though, knowing better. As a young neophyte, he had beheld the human form of his lady once. Her silver hair, her radiant white eyes, her graceful figure, the supple perfection of her ivory skin...

The memory alone added fuel to the raging fire burning in him, making the old priest shift awkwardly and close his eyes in shame.

His queen, the White Abyss, then spoke again:

“Lead the way."

Soon enough, a glorious procession departed from the city. At the head of it, the old priest walked, carrying a golden scepter. Behind him, the mortal incarnation of flame, the Immortal Queen of the First Kingdom, rode atop a magnificent Transcendent beast. Soldiers and chosen members of the priesthood followed — not to assist in the battle, but to witness the glory of their goddess.

It used to be that the White Abyss ruled the Kingdom directly, appearing in front of her people every day. But those days were long past. Now, she spent most of her time in her natural form, the vast ocean of her pristine being blazing in the depths of the great pyramid, filling it with light and immolating heat.

So, it was a rare and glorious occasion to see the great White Abyss descend from her fiery throne and grace the world with her breathtaking presence.

The old priest was full of pride and self-importance... and anxiety, as well.

He wanted everything to go flawlessly, so that his goddess wasn't dishonored by imperfection.

So that she didn't find a flaw in him.

That was why he was enraged and dismayed when, many hours later, a woman who seemed like a homeless beggar appeared in the path of the procession, blocking their way.

The woman was old, with deep lines crossing her weathered face. Her hair was grey, gathered into a messy braid. Her clothes were covered in the red dust of the road, worn and unremarkable, their edges frayed. She had set up a small campfire and was warming her hands in front of it, a simple spear lying on the ground by her side.

They were crossing the desert by then, and the sun was setting... the desert was as vast as the sky. Why couldn't she have set her fire somewhere else instead of in the path of the procession?

What was worse, the woman seemed not to have noticed their approach. She ignored them completely, looking emotionlessly into the flame — the procession would have no choice but to circle around her if they wanted to move forward... unless they were to trample her without ever slowing down. Their glorious queen having to change her path because of a nameless beggar?

A murderous fury ignited in the old priest's chest.

Stepping forward, he raised his scepter, intending to strike the insolent woman down.

"How dare you!"

However, before he could bring the scepter down, a soft radiance ignited under his skin.

This was the light of the White Abyss — her blessing.

A moment later, the old priest opened his mouth and let out a dreadful scream. His skin boiled and blackened, pure white flame escaping from within his body and enveloping him like a storm. His chilling wail ended just as abruptly as it started, and in a second, all that remained of him was a cloud of ash.

The ash was dispelled by the wind.

Sitting atop the towering beast, White Abyss regarded his death with an indifferent expression on her exquisitely beautiful, breathtaking face.

Then, she jumped down to the ground and walked over to the old woman, her white tunic swaying lightly with each of her graceful steps.

Reaching the small fire, she looked down and studied the weathered wanderer. Then, in a voice entirely void of emotion, she asked:

“Have you come to kill me?"

The old woman finally tore her gaze away from the fire and looked at her with a hint of surprise.

“Why would I?"

White Abyss lingered for a moment, then sighed and looked at the sky.

There, the sun was setting, and a scattering of stars was slowly revealing themselves in the velvet darkness of the night. Eventually, she shrugged.

"I just assumed. After all, it is not every day that one of the great gods comes to my realm..."

--- Chapter 3182 ---

White Abyss glanced at the spear lying on the ground near the old woman. It was of simple design, the wooden shaft polished by countless years of use, the sharp blade carved from glistening flint.

She remained silent for a moment.

“I welcome War."

The old woman smiled faintly.

Turning back to the fire, she shrugged.

"Kill you? No. It's not time for that yet."

The great and terrible War God — the goddess of life, warfare, progress, craft, intellect, and humans — leaned closer to the fire.

"I just happened to be passing by. Think nothing of it."

White Abyss studied her with an indifferent expression. Behind her, at a distance, her soldiers and priests were trembling in fear, startled by the cruel death of their senior. Paying them no attention, the radiant incarnation of fire took a step forward and sat across from War, with only the dancing flames separating them.

The goddess spared her a curious glance. She seemed to consider something for a moment, then asked:

“A nephilim ruling a kingdom of humans — the first human kingdom, no less. How unexpected. Tell me, nephilim... that child, Kanakht. What did you do to him?"

White Abyss tilted her head slightly.

"I burned him. He is still burning, somewhere within me."

This incarnation was only a fraction of her. Most of the endless ocean of living flames that mortals called the White Abyss were still contained within the great temple, and at the heart of that temple, a blackened corpse was still being burned by the flames. It had been burning for countless centuries,

endlessly reduced to ash and restored, kept in an immolating cage of rebirth that forbade it from crossing the threshold of life.

That corpse was Kanakht, one of the First Humans — and the first human to have ever become Supreme. He had been cursed by the God of Death, after all, so he couldn't be killed.

He could only be contained.

War chuckled.

“What a cruel fate. Hasn't he suffered enough by now? All that agony, all that pain...”

White Abyss glanced at her, emotionless. However, there seemed to be a hint of incomprehension in her gaze.

After a while, she spoke in an even tone:

"It's just pain.”

Some said that evil stemmed from a lack of knowledge, and that those who knew pain would not visit it upon another. Therefore, pain was the source of compassion. However, White Abyss knew pain better than anyone else in the world, and yet, she was not prone to mercy.

War sighed lightly.

"So, how is it treating you? Playing a god?"

White Abyss frowned, then glanced away with a hint of despondency in her harrowing, radiant eyes.

She remained silent for a long while. Eventually, she said evenly:

“It hasn't been easy."

She glanced at War.

“At the start, I wanted to be a good ruler. I wanted to protect my people from the cruelties of the harsh world and empower them to aspire. I wanted them to pursue their passions without holding back, free and unburdened. I wanted to be kind and compassionate."

The white radiance of her beautiful eyes shone with pristine light.

“And so, I defended them against the Creatures of Corruption. I gave them laws and institutions. I healed their wounds and eradicated their sickness. I fed them, I educated them, I provided for them. No one went hungry in my kingdom, no one suffered the cruel tyranny of need. No one was forced to endure the hardships that they had not chosen to face."

White Abyss fell silent for a moment, then glanced at the fire.

“But in the end, they did not flourish. Instead of prosperity, there was only rot. They grew lazy, entitled, arrogant, and overcome by insatiable greed.They turned on each other and foamed at the mouth in the frenzy to tear their neighbors down. They were consumed by envy, avarice, sloth, depravity, and malignant pride. It is so ugly... it is so distasteful. It is so unlike what I wanted to give them, and what I wanted them to take."

She paused, staring into the dancing flames. After a short while, White Abyss said in an emotionless, frightening tone:

“It makes me want to burn them all."

As she spoke those words, the flames surged, sending a cloud of fiery sparks swirling in the black expanse of the darkening sky. The soldiers and priests who stood in the distance behind her suddenly glanced small and fragile... easily erased with a thought.

War studied the radiant nephilim, a hint of a smile on her lips.

"Why haven't you?"

White Abyss slowly glanced away from the flame and raised her gaze to the stars.

She remained silent for a few long moments. When she spoke, her voice carried a hint of wistful distance.

“How can I? I have lived billions of lives — all of them human. I know all about how ugly humans can be, how distasteful, how deep they can fall into depravity. How fragile their convictions are, how easily they turn on each other. But, still..."

She raised a hand, as if wanting to grasp the stars that burned in the cold embrace of the void.

“They are so beautiful.”

War raised an eyebrow.

"What is beautiful?"

White Abyss smiled faintly.

“Their desires."

She lowered her hand and glanced at War.
